events.title: AI's most powerful CEOs hit the brakes
events.summary: In nine startling hours on Saturday, the four biggest AI labs — which rarely agree on anything — set aside years of feuds and competition to endorse a slower development pace for their models. Their new stance: Prioritize safety over growth , even at a cost. The big picture: AI's unrelenting growth has hit an inflection point with the public, Washington and even the companies building it. Data centers are unpopular . People are panicked about doom scenarios . And 51 days before midterms, legislators suddenly realize there are points to be won by cracking down. Against that backdrop , the industry's most powerful CEOs hit the brakes Saturday. At 10 a.m. ET, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei dropped a 3,800-word essay saying model development needs to be paced , otherwise doom scenarios are possible — like a rogue-agent takeover of the entire internet, which he said could be as soon as six months from now. An hour later, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk shocked the AI chattering class by quoting Amodei's essay on X and saying "Dario is right." Musk — who heads SpaceXAI, formerly xAI — had pointedly not joined previous industry-wide calls for any kind of slowdown. At 12:30 p.m., OpenAI CEO Sam Altman tweeted: "I agree with Dario that we need to pace the frontier." In an interview Friday that was released on Saturday, Altman told Fortune his company won't go public this year, dashing hopes for a blockbuster IPO. He said OpenAI has too much safety work to do and would be better off doing that as a private company. At 7 p.m., Demis Hassabis — the Nobel laureate who co-founded and chairs Google DeepMind, and is Alphabet's chief scientist — tweeted : "Dario's essay points towards the right path forward. The details need working through, but the direction is correct for meeting this critical moment." Between the lines: Publicly putting safety ahead of technological or financial growth may be the industry's only route to avoid a crackdown that's not on its terms. Legislators are begging House Speaker Mike Johnson to stay in session and do something about the "threat" of AI. The more extreme alternative is something like Sen. Bernie Sanders' push to force a pause and make the most advanced AI illegal. Reality check: Most people realize there's too much money at stake to just stop moving forward. But the tradeoff may be between historic riches and slightly less historic riches. Let's see whether they actually agree on what oversight ("embedded third-party evaluators") and "slow" mean, then follow through Friction point: No one in China is having the same kind of we'd-better-stop moment. Influential Silicon Valley tech voices, including former Trump official David Sacks, spent Saturday highlighting the counterargument that slowing down just lets adversaries — with no such safety qualms — catch up. In a late Saturday-night post , Sacks effectively dared OpenAI and Anthropic to voluntarily pace the AI frontier without waiting for the government. "If you don't, we'll know this was just another bid for regulatory capture — or an election-season psyop." Amodei even acknowledged that a safety regime only really works if authoritarian governments come to the table, too. "Pacing within democracies will be limited by the lead that U.S. companies have over authoritarian regimes, chiefly the Chinese Communist Party," he wrote . "If we slow down by more than this amount, then (unpaced) CCP-associated projects will pull ahead, creating significant national security risk." The bottom line: Saturday may go down as the day AI changed — when industry moguls vowed to limit themselves. Read Amodei's essay , "We Must Pace the Frontier."

events.title: The Iran war reveals the limits of BRICS
events.summary: The bloc struggles to translate its economic weight into geopolitical sway. But there may be a silver lining to it. This year’s BRICS summit has wrapped up in New Delhi with the usual promises of deepened cooperation and expanding economic ties. But there was an important absence. Although the US-Israel war on Iran has affected most of BRICS’ 11 members and 10 partner countries, the declaration issued by the bloc did not address it directly. Nor did it condemn the United States, which – objectively speaking – is the aggressor state in the conflict. The wording allowed all members to remain inside the same diplomatic tent. It also revealed just how difficult it is for BRICS to turn shared dissatisfaction with the Western-led order into coordinated geopolitical action. The problem was already visible months before the summit. In May, the BRICS foreign ministers’ meeting in New Delhi failed to produce a common position on the war on Iran. The outcome document acknowledged differences among members and avoided naming either the US or Israel. Iran wanted the group to condemn the US and Israeli military campaign, while the UAE opposed language that ignored Iranian attacks and its own security concerns. That failure was more than a diplomatic embarrassment. It was a clear sign of the political cost of BRICS expansion. The group’s enlargement has increased its global reach, but it has also imported regional rivalries into the organisation itself. Iran and the UAE are a particularly clear example. Both belong to BRICS, yet their strategic calculations in the Middle East collide. Their participation in the same organisation therefore creates a built-in ceiling on how far the group can go in confronting a conflict that directly affects both. The September summit produced a declaration, but the compromise was telling. Rather than taking a clear, strong position, BRICS became a platform for managing disagreement. The episode therefore suggests that the central problem facing the bloc is not a lack of economic or diplomatic weight. It is the difficulty of converting that weight into a single geopolitical instrument. While BRICS has emerged out of a desire to challenge the US-dominated world order, it has failed to reach a common position on Washington. That is because its members have divergent interests when it comes to dealing with the US. India illustrates the dilemma most clearly. New Delhi sees BRICS as a vehicle for strategic autonomy, not as an alliance against the US. It is deepening its relationship with Washington, participating in the Quad and maintaining extensive defence and economic ties with Western partners. At the same time, it remains deeply engaged with Russia and China. For India, the value of BRICS lies partly in preserving room for manoeuvre between competing centres of power. Turning BRICS into an anti-American bloc would undermine precisely that strategic flexibility. China and Russia also have reasons to avoid transforming BRICS into a mechanism for direct confrontation with the US. For Russia, BRICS is unquestionably an important platform for reducing the political and economic impact of Western economic pressure. Yet, pursuing more aggressive policies through military alliances could push Moscow into a conflict with the US and NATO – something it wants to avoid at all costs. For China, the calculation is even more complex. Beijing wants a stronger multipolar order and greater influence for the Global South. It also wants to reduce the structural advantages enjoyed by the US in global finance, trade and international institutions. But China has little reason to turn every BRICS dispute into a binary confrontation with Washington. The US remains an important market for its exports and an important factor in global trade. Brazil and Indonesia add another layer of complexity. Brasilia wants a more representative international system, greater development finance and stronger bargaining power for developing countries, but has little incentive to turn BRICS into an instrument of Chinese or Russian geopolitical strategy. Similarly, Jakarta sees BRICS as a way to widen its strategic and economic options rather than as a vehicle for choosing sides. BRICS is caught in what appears to be a polycentric trap. Its greatest strength is its diversity. That diversity gives the group legitimacy across regions that have historically had little influence over the architecture of global governance. But the same diversity makes collective geopolitical action difficult. Every new member adds economic resources, diplomatic reach and political legitimacy. It also adds another set of national interests that must be accommodated. This explains why BRICS is more likely to become a powerful bargaining coalition than a coherent geopolitical bloc.

events.title: The AI doomsday debate intensifies
events.summary: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei have called for a slowdown in AI. Emma McIntyre/Getty Images, FABRICE COFFRINI/AFP via Getty Images This post originally appeared in the BI Today newsletter. You can sign up for Business Insider's daily newsletter here . Existential angst What do you do if you feel like you're helping build something that could contribute to the end of humanity? This is the existential question confronting the AI industry, a debate that only intensified after Jacob Coxon, an Anthropic researcher, quit last week with a stark warning . He said AI giants are "gambling with our lives" and that the people building the technology "earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade." The swift reaction to Coxon's warning boiled over on Saturday when the leaders of the biggest AI companies publicly agreed on what should happen next. In a Saturday essay, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei says he's "become convinced" the breakneck pace of advancement must change and proposed a three-step solution to ensure the tech's safety. Shortly afterward, Elon Musk and Sam Altman publicly aligned with Amodei's plan in a rare sign of support. "Dario is right," Musk tweeted. Altman agreed, too, saying the pace of development has been a "primary topic" of discussion at OpenAI in recent weeks. Altman also said OpenAI might not move forward with an IPO this year. "Right now would be an ill-advised moment to go public," he said in a Fortune interview. As fears over AI safety intensify, employees at Anthropic and OpenAI have also been speaking out. My colleague Sarah Needleman reported on a big question facing many concerned AI employees : Should they quit or stay amid fears of an AI apocalypse? Some AI workers believe they can do more good by staying on the inside. That means raising concerns, pushing for safeguards, and trying to influence decisions before they are made. Others worry that staying at these companies only helps legitimize a race that some believe is getting dangerously out of control. BI's Alistair Bar explored some of these theories in this week's edition of AI Insider — you can subscribe here to his weekly newsletter. Are employees at the big AI lab companies better off leaving or staying if they feel like their work is contributing to a possible AI apocalypse? Send me a note at srussolillo@businessinsider.com and let me know what you think. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: The Houthis’ escalation in Yemen could flop
events.summary: The Houthis and Iran are seeking to gain leverage, but they may instead get a unified front in the Red Sea. The speed of the Houthi advance along the Red Sea coast has changed the strategic landscape. After capturing Mocha, Houthi forces moved into Dhubab and reached Mayyun, or Perim Island, at the narrowest point of the Bab al-Mandeb strait. These are not peripheral gains. They give the movement unprecedented leverage over one of the world’s most important maritime corridors. This latest escalation in Yemen is not simply another episode in its long civil war. It is also not simply an escalatory move by Iran against Gulf states, particularly Saudi Arabia. It is at once a struggle for the control of Yemen, a renewed confrontation between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia, and another front in the wider war involving Iran, Israel and the United States. Several factors contributed to it, including the false sense of balance of power in Yemen, the Houthi desire to secure a stronger negotiating position, and the spillover of the Iran war. The latest offensive cannot be understood without considering the false sense of peace that preceded it. A United Nations-mediated truce took effect in April 2022. Although it formally expired six months later, Saudi Arabia and the Houthis largely maintained a de facto ceasefire. Saudi and Omani delegations travelled to Sanaa a year later. In June 2023, direct flights resumed between Sanaa and Saudi Arabia to carry Yemeni pilgrims to Hajj, the first such flights since 2016. In September 2023, a senior Houthi delegation visited Riyadh for talks on ending the war. These were important confidence-building measures. But they also encouraged the dangerous assumption that Yemen’s conflict was gradually resolving itself. The internationally recognised government appears to have mistaken the absence of major fighting for a durable balance of power. Despite repeated talk since April 2025 of an offensive along the western coast, its leaders remained divided, and its armed formations answered to competing commands. Rather than using the pause to rebuild legitimacy, improve governance and establish a coherent military structure, the government and its supporters became complacent. The Houthis used the same period very differently. The reduction in fighting gave them time and strategic space to consolidate their administration, reorganise their forces, expand their missile and drone capabilities, and recruit on a vast scale. A 2024 report by United Nations experts estimated that the Houthis’ fighting strength had risen from approximately 220,000 in 2022 to 350,000, compared with just 30,000 in 2015. Such figures must be treated cautiously, but they indicate how extensively the movement expanded during what others regarded as a period of peace. It should be noted that this process also involved documented coercion and child recruitment. The genocide in Gaza also gave the Houthis a powerful mobilising cause. Palestine is close to the heart of almost every Yemeni, cutting across many of the country’s political, regional and sectarian divisions. By presenting their attacks on Israel and their Red Sea operations as direct action in defence of Gaza, the Houthis portrayed themselves not merely as one party in Yemen’s civil war, but as perhaps the only Arab force willing and able to impose a cost on Israel. Iranian deterrence strategy v Houthi priorities For the first six months of the war, Iran appears to have tried to keep the Red Sea from becoming another major front. It had a clear interest in keeping Saudi Arabia and Egypt (the two pivotal Arab powers bordering the Red Sea) outside a US-led military alignment. Renewed Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia or commercial shipping risked pushing Riyadh and Cairo closer to Washington. It is reasonable to assume that Tehran initially pressed the Houthis not to provoke Saudi Arabia. But the Saudi strike on Sanaa International Airport in July changed the calculation. Reportedly intended to prevent an Iranian aircraft from landing, it gave the Houthis a reason to retaliate and evidence that restraint would not protect them. Iran may not have wanted a Saudi-Houthi confrontation, but once the Houthis decided to respond, Tehran could hardly demand that they remain passive without undermining the credibility of an alliance it had spent years cultivating. The escalation also serves Iran’s interests. Its disruption of Gulf supplies was losing some of its force as Washington and its partners helped the international market adjust through alternative suppliers and routes bypassing Hormuz . Oil prices are high, but the shortage Iran may have hoped to create has not fully materialised, while additional sanctions and the blockade are beginning to bite.

events.title: I travel often, but just took my first luxury cruise. The food was great, and it was easy to relax, but there was 1 unexpected drawback.
events.summary: The author went on her first cruise at 49. Courtesy of Alesandra Dubin Though I travel often, I had never been on a cruise. I had misconceptions about this popular way of travel. All that changed when my husband and I went on a luxury cruise for my 49th birthday. Even as a seasoned traveler , it took me nearly five decades to get on a cruise ship at all. I had never been particularly curious about cruising and had some pretty unflattering ideas about what it involved: heaping buffets of dubious food, brightly colored drinks, crowded decks, and a style of travel that seemed much too packaged for me. Then, this summer, I spent nine nights traveling through Northern Europe and discovered that much of what I thought I knew about cruising was wrong. My husband and I went on a cruise for my 49th birthday. The author realized she had some misconceptions about cruises. Courtesy of Alesandra Dubin My husband and I sailed aboard Crystal Serenity from Southampton to Copenhagen, a voyage on which I would celebrate my 49th birthday. And this was admittedly a very cushy introduction: I stayed in a Sapphire Veranda Suite with a walk-in closet, veranda, and butler service. So I'm certainly not suggesting my experience represents every cruise. But as someone who typically takes complicated, high-effort trips, I found these were the things that surprised me most about my first one. I couldn't believe how easy everything was. Planning a cruise was much easier than the author's typical way of traveling. Courtesy of Alesandra Dubin I'm accustomed to doing a lot of work when I travel. I tend to build ambitious itineraries involving multiple cities, hotels, trains, flights, restaurant reservations, and activities. I love that kind of travel, but there are a lot of logistics involved — and as the mom and travel planner in chief, I'm usually the one managing them all. Cruising took an astonishing amount of that effort away. I unpacked once, put everything in the closet, slid my empty suitcase under the bed, and didn't deal with it again for nine nights. While I slept, ate dinner, or watched a show, my hotel was effortlessly transporting me to another country. The rest felt similarly organized. An on-ship newsletter featured printed itineraries that told me exactly what would be happening on board the following day. Excursions were coordinated around the ship's arrival and departure. Restaurants, entertainment, and activities were steps from my room. I hadn't realized just how much mental and physical energy I normally spend administering my own trips until I didn't have to. The food was incredible. They were pleasantly surprised by the food on the cruise. Courtesy of Alesandra Dubin Cruise food , in my imagination, was mostly about quantity: enormous buffets of mediocre food feeding thousands of people at once. What I encountered on Crystal was very different. The main dining room didn't repeat dishes, so you could always count on something new to try. Beyond that, my favorite meals came from places that I'd consider hot restaurants even in my buzzy hometown of Los Angeles. Umi Uma, created by Nobu Matsuhisa, served sophisticated Japanese food and sushi. Osteria d'Ovidio offered seriously high-end Italian cooking. Obviously, this was a luxury ship , and I wouldn't assume every cruise serves food like this one did. But it thoroughly dismantled my assumption that cruise dining necessarily meant choosing among endless ho-hum chafing dishes at a buffet. I couldn't believe I sometimes preferred staying on board to sightseeing. The author was surprised that sometimes, she wanted to stay on board instead of going on excursions. Courtesy of Alesandra Dubin Before this trip, I couldn't understand why anyone would travel somewhere only to spend the day on a ship. But the ship turned me into such a person. There were history lectures, art classes, live performances, a spa, pools, a movie theater, and a casino. I entered a $100 blackjack tournament on a whim and somehow came in third (I'll be getting mileage out of this proud moment for years to come). The ultimate test came when we docked in Rotterdam. We had booked an excursion to Amsterdam that would take most of the day, but we decided to cancel it to spend more time on board. I never would have seen that coming. I actually relaxed — something I'm not very good at doing on trips. Traveling by cruise offered a nice change of pace. Courtesy of Alesandra Dubin I love travel, but my tendency to cram a lot into every trip means I frequently return home exhausted. On the cruise, I slept like an absolute baby. (My husband suggested it might be the gentle motion of the sea that lulled me.) In fact, I slept in so late that I ended up setting my alarm for 10 a.m. I knew I'd miss regular breakfast, but I didn't want to miss the late-riser breakfast from 10 to 11 — or sleep through a day when there were things on board I actually wanted to do. Without transportation to arrange, hotels to change, or a packed sightseeing agenda to manage, I settled into a pace I rarely allow myself while traveling. For once, the words "travel" and "vacation" actually felt synonymous. I sometimes questioned how deeply I was experiencing the destinations. However, sometimes she felt she wasn't truly experiencing the places they docked. Courtesy of Alesandra Dubin For all the things I loved about cruising, one of my original reservations did bear out. I usually think of travel as a way to experience a place and its culture. I like wandering neighborhoods, eating local cuisine, figuring out public transportation , and having the kinds of unplanned interactions that happen when you're actually immersed in a destination (even when they're stressful). A port stop is different. We visited some incredible places, and we were generally there for only a few hours before returning to the ship. There was less time for wandering, spontaneity, or meaningful cultural exchange. In that sense, this cruise felt more like a true vacation than the kind of travel I typically do. And, as it turns out, I really needed and enjoyed that. But I did sometimes wonder how much I could say I'd truly experienced a destination after seeing it within the relatively controlled framework of a port day. So if my primary goal were to deeply get to know a place, I'd still choose to stay there rather than visit it by ship. But I loved the shipboard experience, and it turned out to be one of the best trips I've taken in recent memory. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Surging inflation puts interest rates back in focus as policymakers meet in Japan, US and UK
events.summary: Iran war and turbulent global bond markets add to pressure as rate decisions loom this week in major western economies Economics viewpoint: perilous UK economic conditions trace back to Trump Central bankers in economies including the US, Japan and the UK will face a moment of truth this week, as surging inflation raises the prospect of higher interest rates. Policymakers in all three countries will set rates in the next seven days against the backdrop of turbulent global bond markets . In particular, investors will be watching closely to see if Kevin Warsh, the new chair of the US Federal Reserve , can face down Donald Trump’s demands for rate cuts and instead persuade Fed governors to raise them on Wednesday. Warsh was handpicked by the US president , who has repeatedly demanded lower interest rates. In a Truth Social post this month, Trump claimed the US should have the “LOWEST RATE of any country in the World”. He added: “The Fed Board, with its great new leader, must get smart – BE PATRIOTS for a change.” However, the central bank’s board of governors is having to contend with a renewed rise in oil prices after the US-Iran conflict intensified again . The cost of a barrel of crude surged past $100 last week for the first time since July, as the strait of Hormuz remained all but closed to tanker traffic and Houthi rebels advanced along the Red Sea coast, threatening to choke off Saudi oil supplies. Oil prices eased slightly on Friday amid hopes of fresh talks to reopen the waterway but remained well above levels in the summer, when Middle East hostilities temporarily abated. Higher energy costs are expected to feed a fresh rise in US inflation, which has been above the Fed’s 2% target for more than five years. In a speech this month, Warsh said without continued progress towards the target, Fed policymakers would have “work to do”. Data published on Friday showed annual US inflation unchanged at 3.4%. Andrew Bailey, the Bank of England governor, has struck a calm note about above-target inflation in the UK, saying rising mortgage rates have done some of the work of a rate rise without the Bank taking action. Markets and economists are predicting the Bank will hold rates at 3.75% on Thursday. However, three of the nine members of the Bank’s monetary policy committee (MPC) voted for a rate rise in July , and data published on Friday showing stronger-than-expected economic growth could amplify fears about inflation. Thomas Pugh, the chief economist at RSM, a consultancy firm, said the latest rise in energy prices had “materially increased the chance that the MPC will eventually follow other major central banks and raise rates”. But he predicted a “hawkish hold” from the Bank when the MPC convenes on Thursday: a decision to leave rates unchanged, but with the published minutes pointing to potential future rises. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Financial markets are betting on four UK rate rises over the next 12 months – up from the three they were expecting before the latest surge in oil prices. In Tokyo, Bank of Japan (BoJ) policymakers will announce their decision on Friday and are widely expected to raise interest rates, validating the recent recovery of the yen on foreign exchanges. A quarter-point increase in the BoJ’s policy rate, to 1.25%, would take it to levels not seen for more than 30 years, since Japan first began fighting an extended battle against deflation, or falling prices. The US Treasury joined Japanese authorities in intervening in foreign exchange markets to support the yen in July and Scott Bessent, the Treasury secretary, has made it clear that he expects rates to rise. At an event at Southern Methodist University in Texas on Tuesday, Bessent said: “When we intervene with the Japanese yen, I have pretty good insight into what the Bank of Japan is going to do, what Japanese policymakers are going to do. I have asymmetric information. I am the house now. You can bet against me if you want.” The European Central Bank raised interest rates on Thursday . Christine Lagarde, its president, said: “The conflict in the Middle ​East continues ​to ⁠generate inflation pressures, and inflation is set to ​remain well above target for ​an ⁠extended period.”

events.title: OpenAI rules out IPO this year as Altman, Musk & Amodei warn AI is moving too fast
events.summary: In an interview with Fortune published Saturday, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said that an IPO now would be "ill-advised." Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei also published an essay on Saturday urging AI companies to intentionally pace how quickly they improve model capabilities. Elon Musk and Sam Altman signaled their support of Amodei’s proposal. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman now says his company will not go public this year, citing growing concerns about AI safety. In an interview with Fortune published Saturday , Altman said that an IPO now would be "ill-advised." The decision pushes one of the most anticipated IPOs in history until at least 2027 and gives the clearest sign yet that mounting concerns about increasingly powerful AI are beginning to reshape the industry's business plans. OpenAI CFO Sarah Friar told employees just last month that the company would likely go public in 2027 or even sooner, if "our business continues to inflect." Altman's comments came on the same day that Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei published an essay urging AI companies to slow how quickly they improve their most advanced models. Altman and Elon Musk quickly backed the proposal in social media posts, an unusual show of agreement among three fierce rivals. In his essay, Amodei proposed a three-step plan aimed at tempering the pace of development without "sacrificing commercial advantage or the United States' lead in AI." Anthropic is actively gearing up for what is expected to be a historic IPO , though the company has not officially disclosed when it plans to debut. The sudden alignment among Altman, Amodei and Musk shows how quickly concern over AI has moved from the margins to the center of the industry — and is now beginning to collide with its enormous commercial ambitions. The essay urged artificial intelligence companies to pace how quickly they improve model capabilities. The move comes amid a growing chorus of researchers calling for a coordinated deceleration. Amodei proposed a three-step plan that he said will help temper the pace of development without "sacrificing commercial advantage or the United States' lead in AI," though he conceded that some steps may be easier to achieve than others. Pressure is building in Washington, where lawmakers in both parties are calling for new AI safeguards and demanding tech leaders testify after a rash of cyberattacks were carried out without direct human control. Beyond the nation's capital, state and local officials are also confronting growing outrage against AI data centers and their demands on power, water and communities. With midterm elections approaching, AI is becoming a key issue for both parties. Anthropic has "unilaterally" committed to the first step of the plan, Amodei said, which grants third-party evaluators employee-level access to the company to verify safety practices and report incidents. The second step encourages leading AI companies within democratic countries to coordinate and establish common safety standards, and the third calls for coordination between democratic governments and authoritarian governments. "To be clear, pacing does not mean halting model training or technical progress, but ensuring companies take adequate time to align and safeguard their models, and for third party evaluators to confirm this," Amodei wrote. The essay landed after an Anthropic researcher set off a firestorm on social media this week by announcing he quit his job at the company. Jacob Coxon, who has also worked as a researcher at Anthropic's chief rival, OpenAI, said he resigned out of concern that Anthropic and OpenAI are "gambling with our lives." He said the people building AI "earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade." While extreme, concerns about the potential for AI to cause human extinction or other catastrophic events are not new in AI research circles. In 2023, for instance, prominent AI researchers and executives, including Amodei and OpenAI's Altman , signed a statement that said, "Mitigating the risk of extinction from AI should be a global priority alongside other societal-scale risks such as pandemics and nuclear war." Amodei said Saturday that while pausing or slowing AI development has been floated since 2023, it made "little sense" to do so at that time. He said models were not powerful enough to take action in the real world at that point, and they were also not yet capable of "significant deception, manipulation, cheating, or cyberattacks." My desire to achieve these benefits is undimmed," Amodei wrote.

events.title: I started a real estate brokerage at 26 and am nearing $1 billion in deals. I have no work-life balance and still knock on doors.
events.summary: Jordan Karp founded his own brokerage in his 20s and is always working — even when he's off the clock. Jordan Braun Jordan Karp launched his own brokerage at 26 and has a transaction volume of nearly $1 billion. Karp goes above and beyond for clients by ensuring around-the-clock availability. He works with celebrities and high-net-worth clients, but isn't too proud to still knock on doors. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Jordan Karp, 30, founder and CEO of Jordan Karp LLC, a real estate brokerage in South Florida. Karp started his own brokerage at 26 years old and has nearly reached $1 billion in transaction volume. The following has been edited for length and clarity. I started my business at the beginning of 2023. Before, I was working on investing for my family and creating a portfolio of acquiring diverse assets from 2020 to 2022. I was cold-calling for properties to acquire, invest, assemble, buy, lease, and manage across all asset classes. I was doing it for industrial, commercial, retail, residential, single-family, development sites, creative, and opportunistic multidimensional strategic assets across Florida. I was brokering deals for myself on the side where I saw value in the market, and did that until the end of 2022. Then I started my business full-time. My transaction volume is about $500 million from January until now, and about $1 billion lifetime. I love my job because no day is the same. Here's a glimpse at what my workdays look like. I catch up with clients on restaurant rooftops, boats, and the padel court I have all different types of clients. I have celebrity clients and I also have private equity clients. I have clients who've sold businesses, CEOs, people in private businesses, founders, chairmen of businesses, lawyers, managers. One of my clients and close friends, Austin Rosen, manages Post Malone, and he has a private restaurant rooftop at the Electric Feel Studios in Miami, where I'll usually have client meetings, dinners, and spend a lot of time. I work with a lot of music artists, managers, and people in the music industry, and we'll meet at Feel. I'm very dynamic, and I'm very adaptive to where I meet clients. It's definitely important to meet people in person, whether it be at the office, on the padel court , in the street, or at a certain property. I usually work with a boat or yacht company, and they service me whenever I have a client in town to look at different properties on the water. Karp often takes clients on boats to show them properties on the water. Courtesy of Jordan Karp. If the client is not familiar with Miami or Florida as a whole, I'll take them by boat or a yacht. We'll start at the southernmost point of Miami and go all the way to Bal Harbour, the northernmost part. I'll give them a full education and information about the market, what properties trade for, the price per foot, the trends of where things are going, and they can see the level of houses. I'm available to my clients whenever they need me — even at 3 a.m. There's no difference to me between 12 a.m. and 12 p.m. — my phone is going off all day. I've taken calls at all hours of the night; I've done 2 a.m., I've done 3 a.m. When I was selling the SLS Brickell Hotel for $55 million in 2023, I was selling that for the Royal Family of Qatar, and they were based in London. I represented the seller, and I also represented the buyer, which was a private Albanian group, Kastrati Group. They were in Albania and traveling through Eastern Europe, and the main office for the Royal Family of Qatar was in London. So I was up all hours of the night. They would call me at 4 a.m., 3 a.m., and 2 a.m. They would send me documents. I'd have to get on calls with them; they were in the same time zone as each other, or slightly different ones, but a closer time zone than where I was. My work-life balance is work, work, work. My work and my life, and the balance of working within my life, are vertically integrated. I live to work. I don't work to live. For me, this is fun. It's not work. A $24 million Miami Beach, Florida, property brokered by Karp. I'll go on a run from where I live on North Bay Road up through to Allison Island , to La Gorce Island. I get a running perspective when I'm running by them and see, "Oh, that's an address I should keep in mind." Then I'll be taking calls for work while I'm doing that. So I'll be fielding different properties, but also fielding calls and working on the progression of that all at the same time while running those routes of the neighborhoods. Sometimes the important call comes in the middle of that time or when you're outreaching to a client, and they're busy, and the worst time for you is the best time for them. You have to take that call in that moment and bring three different people who have three different time schedules together. You're in the middle of your workout. But what you do doesn't really matter compared to what the greater goal is. Then, from the workout, I'll shower, and it'll be 10 o'clock at night, and then I'll decompress from 11 p.m. to 12 a.m. and be on my phone and still be available for calls, and look at calls that I missed while I was in the shower. events.title: Grandma's 72 and still working to support her children — and theirs
events.summary: Joann Ernst has played a "motherly" role in her grandchildren's lives. Roy de la Cruz for BI Joann Ernst, 72, shook her head as her older grandson decapitated an action figure. The other laid out puzzle pieces in a line, surrounded by a sea of toys. "You have to put all the Play-Doh back in the container so it doesn't dry out," Ernst called out to the 5- and 7-year olds. Ernst is not the boys' legal guardian . She's spent the past two years living with her son Jack, helping with her grandsons on weekends. Jack had struggled to work after losing an arm in an accident, so Ernst took a job in the special education department of a local school, paid his rent, and spent weekends shopping for the boys and disciplining them "as a mother would." Ernst watches on as her son, Jack, helps the boys with their technology. Roy de la Cruz for BI In June, she moved back to Oregon from Connecticut. She needed to help her daughter, Joanna, with her children in the same way she's been helping Jack and his boys. "I wish I could just be a grandmother, but I also discipline, school them, feed them, and provide a home for them," Ernst said. "I enjoy it immensely, but I'm unable to retire, and my retirement money is slowly being spent." For some grandparents, helping adult children through illness, job loss, addiction, or other crises means taking on far more than occasional babysitting. They become the family's financial and practical backstop, spending down savings, delaying retirement , or going back to work to help support both adult children and grandchildren. Business Insider wants to hear from grandparents caring for their grandchildren and older Americans caring for younger loved ones. Share your story by filling out this quick form . This year, Business Insider has spoken with more than 60 grandparents and great- grandparents raising young children or helping adult children get back on their feet, just when they thought they'd be retiring. Some have legal custody of their grandchildren. Others, like Ernst, have no official parenting roles but pay bills, provide care, and prepare them for a good life. Census data show that more than 1.1 million US grandparents 60 and older were at least part-time caregivers for their grandchildren as of 2024. The boys have been treated to many gifts by their grandmother. Roy de la Cruz for BI "Where is my Barbie?" her older grandson asks. "Barbie is long gone," Ernst replies, adding that she threw her out after her leg fell off. "She's in the city dump." "Can you buy a new Barbie?" "I'll talk about it later with your dad." Ernst raised three children, mostly as a single mother . Around 2016, her daughter Joanna developed a debilitating kidney condition that left her hospitalized for months. Ernst helped care for Joanna's children and received a small state caregiver income. "It never ceases to amaze me how, despite everything, my mom has always been there for my kids and me," Joanna, 43, says. "She always wanted to make us thrive." In 2024, Ernst moved to Connecticut to support Jack after his injury. She found a house with $1,500 monthly rent payments and began her teaching job. Now that she's returned to Oregon, she continues to pay the mortgage on her current house in Connecticut so Jack and his sons can stay there. She also works 25 hours a week as a paid caregiver for Joanna's son with autism and helps to support him financially. Ernst has supported Jack financially. Roy de la Cruz for BI Ernst has tried to balance being frugal with the instinct to give her grandchildren small treats, but even going out to the movies can become a budget decision. This isn't what she expected retirement to be. "If you look at a traditional grandparent, they get to have their grandkids for the day, take them out, and give them ice cream," Joann says. "I'm never at that point because I'm constantly disciplining and explaining things. You're never relaxed." Althea Smith, 65, has faced a more formal version of the same pressure. She is raising her grandson as his legal guardian while also providing long-term care for her own parents. Smith has a job as a full-time support worker for older adults and said she doesn't expect to fully retire soon. Ernst often would take the boys out to eat. Roy de la Cruz for BI "I want to see the world and take a cruise," she said. "I miss being able to go wherever I want. My grandson will be 18 in four years, and then I'll be able to think more about myself." Ernst's kitchen table may be filled with receipts and bills — groceries, the mortgage, and a car loan — but she says it's money well-spent. She tries to avoid thinking about her diminishing nest egg. "I know it'll all work out," Joann said, watching the boys dash across the living room. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Read the memo: PwC US is planning big changes to its offshore structure in India
events.summary: PwC is making changes to its offshore delivery center model. Artur Widak/NurPhoto via Getty Images PwC US is shaking up its offshore delivery center model in India. The US firm is planning a joint venture with PwC India, merging its offshore center with its India operation. The move will improve access to talent and technology, CEO Paul Griggs said in a memo to staff. PwC US is overhauling its offshore delivery structure in India, bringing its local operations closer to PwC India's consulting business. The US firm and PwC India plan to form a new joint venture that will merge PwC US's India-based offshoring hubs — known as Acceleration Centers, or ACs — with PwC India's consulting arm, according to an internal memo sent to staff on Saturday by the US CEO, Paul Griggs . Those hubs provide specialist talent and overnight support to US teams and operate independently of PwC India's operations. Creating a joint venture will help PwC compete more effectively as a global network, Griggs said in the memo. The tie-up would drive growth and create new opportunities, improve access to talent and capabilities, and bring the firm's "technology, engineering and AI capabilities together at greater scale," said Griggs. PwC announced the agreement early Sunday morning after Business Insider contacted the company. Neither PwC US nor PwC India responded to requests for comment. The transaction is expected to close in the first half of 2027, subject to closing conditions and regulatory approvals, the memo said. Paul Griggs, CEO of PwC US Mandel NGAN / AFP via Getty Images Professional services firms have long used offshoring centers in lower-cost regions such as India, Argentina, and the Philippines. The hubs help firms keep client costs down, tap specialist skills, and offer round-the-clock delivery. During a consulting or auditing project, US-based employees send non-client-facing work to offshore teams in different time zones to be completed overnight. A PwC US consultant told Business Insider that they turn to PwC India when the India AC does not have enough capacity. But doing so can create delays, because the firms must renegotiate rates and terms of the work. The joint venture could speed up that process by removing "the middle man, PwC AC," they said. The joint venture also signals closer collaboration between PwC's US and Indian firms — a meaningful shift for a network built around separate national member firms. Like its fellow Big Four competitors —KPMG, Deloitte, and EY — PwC operates as a global network of legally separate firms rather than a single company. That structure is particularly important on the audit side of the business, where firms must navigate local regulations and independence requirements. "The firms that win will be the ones that stop thinking about markets, capabilities, and delivery as separate pieces," said Griggs in a press release on Sunday. The move isn't about where work gets done, but about offering clients a more seamless experience and the "best of PwC," he added. The firm is aiming to build a more globally integrated consulting model. In April, the Financial Times reported that PwC UK planned to merge its risk and consulting businesses as part of that strategy. Read the full memo sent to US staff on Saturday here: Team, Tomorrow, PwC US and PwC India will sign an agreement to establish a new joint venture that will bring together PwC US Advisory's India-based Acceleration Centers and PwC India's Consulting business. This combination will drive growth and strengthen how we serve increasingly global clients. India is one of the world's most important growth markets and a source of world-class talent and capabilities. Bringing these businesses closer together will help us connect those strengths—more effectively expanding access to talent and capabilities, bringing our technology, engineering, and AI capabilities together at greater scale, and creating new opportunities for our clients and across our businesses. Over time, the joint venture will strengthen our ability to bring more of PwC to our clients wherever those capabilities sit, support clients as they grow and operate across markets, and compete more effectively as a global network. Signing is an important milestone and the beginning of the next phase. We expect the transaction to close in the first half of calendar year 2027, subject to closing conditions and regulatory approvals. Until then, teams will continue to serve clients and operate through existing structures and ways of working. Please keep this information confidential until the external announcement is issued on Sunday evening, Eastern Time. We're excited about what this joint venture will unlock for our clients, our people and PwC. Paul Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: BRICS summit 2026: What are the key takeaways?
events.summary: The 11-member bloc, which accounts for 40% of global GDP, avoids condemning US-Israel war on Iran, showing divisions within the group. Leaders of the BRICS group of nations unanimously adopted a joint declaration on the first day of the two-day summit in the Indian capital, New Delhi, despite divisions among members over the wars in Iran and Ukraine. The New Delhi Declaration, adopted on Saturday, called for restraint in the Middle East but avoided condemning the US-Israeli strikes or Iran’s targeting of Gulf countries in the region. It also criticised the global trade war without naming the United States. list 1 of 3 Putin, Pezeshkian in India for BRICS summit clouded by Iran and Ukraine war list 2 of 3 Next BRICS summit can get an Iran ceasefire list 3 of 3 Multipolarity gives middle powers more choices, but fewer guarantees Chinese President Xi Jinping and his Russian counterpart, Vladimir Putin, were among the leaders attending the gathering of the 11-member bloc in New Delhi at a time of global upheaval caused by the US-Israel war on Iran, Trump’s tariff war and the US’s unilateral decisions to promote its foreign policy. Al Jazeera’s Um-e-Kulsoom Shariff, reporting from New Delhi, said the group “steered clear” of naming any countries, even on the issue of wide-ranging US tariffs. “We’ve seen BRICS countries who have been targeted, be it India, Russia, China, or any other, but they have stayed clear,” she reported. “While they said unilateral tariffs are condemned and they work against international law, they have not named the US. So India had to keep in mind that it has bilateral trade relations with other countries, and so do others.” Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi said BRICS had reached a “coming of age” moment and called on the Global South to become a “rule-shaper” rather than simply accept rules set elsewhere. Here are key takeaways from the declaration from the summit: BRICS was founded in 2006 by Brazil, Russia, India and China, mainly as an economic forum. South Africa joined the grouping four years later. It has since expanded to include Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia and Indonesia. The BRICS nations constitute nearly half the world’s population and account for approximately 40 percent of global gross domestic product (GDP). The bloc has sought greater influence for developing economies in institutions traditionally dominated by Western powers and has pushed for reforms to bodies, including the World Bank, the International Monetary Fund and the World Trade Organization. Conveying India’s position, Modi insisted that the bloc should not be interpreted simply as an anti-Western project. “BRICS is not against anyone,” he said, while arguing that the Global South should play a bigger role in shaping global governance. The war was one of the biggest tests of whether the expanded BRICS could reach a common position. Leaders expressed “deep concern over the continued escalation of tensions” in the Middle East and called for “maximum restraint”, while urging countries to avoid actions that could further aggravate the situation. It did not mention the US, Israel, Iran or the Gulf states explicitly. China’s Xi said in a statement the war “does not serve the common interests of the international community”, and called for a political settlement and a permanent and comprehensive ceasefire. In May, BRICS foreign ministers failed to agree on a joint statement amid differences over the war. Iran is a member of BRICS, as is the UAE, which has faced Iranian attacks during the conflict. Former Indian Foreign Secretary Nirupama Menon Rao said New Delhi scored a “significant diplomatic success” in securing a declaration despite “sharp differences between Iran and the UAE”. “Consensus was preserved, but only through carefully generalised language. In this, BRICS’s value and its limitation was exposed: it can keep difficult conversations alive and affirm broad principles, but it struggles to assign responsibility or organise collective action when there is the occasional collision of the interests of its members,” she posted on X. The declaration also raised concern over deliberate attacks on civilian infrastructure and peaceful nuclear facilities protected by International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) safeguards – language that could be seen as an indirect criticism of US and Israeli attacks on Iranian nuclear sites. During the 12-day war in 2025, the US bombed three main Iranian nuclear facilities at Natanz, Isfahan and Fordow. Praveen Donthi, senior analyst at the International Crisis Group, said expectations for the BRICS summit were low due to geopolitical turbulence and clashing strategic interests. “The members, invested in the success of this non-Western grouping, would be reasonably satisfied with the modest outcome,” he said.

The company made a quarterly cash distribution of 34 cents per common unit for the second quarter of 2026. At an annualized payment of $1.36 per common unit, ET offers a yield of 6.3%. Recently, JPMorgan analyst Jeremy Tonet reiterated a buy rating on Energy Transfer stock and slightly raised his price target to $25 from $24. The analyst noted that the company delivered a strong Q2 beat across all key metrics. The 5-star analyst added that the company "tightened" its capex to $5.6 billion–$5.9 billion and expects capex above $5 billion annually through 2029, given solid opportunities. His ratings have been successful 64% of the time, delivering an average return of 12.8%. See Permian Resources Statistics on TipRanks. Moving on to Sempra Energy ( SRE ), a utility holding company. Earlier this month, the company declared a quarterly dividend of $0.6575 per share, payable on October 15. At an annualized dividend of $2.63 per share, SRE stock offers a yield of about 3.1%. Recently, Jefferies analyst Julien Dumoulin-Smith upgraded SRE stock to Buy from Hold but slightly lowered the price target to $97 from $101. The 5-star analyst noted that Sempra stock is trading at a price/earnings multiple that is 14% below its electric peers due to concerns about Texas transmission capital expenditure and the failure of California legislation. Smith noted that the derating of weaker California peers PG&E (PCG) and Edison International (EIX) is weighing on the sum-of-the-parts (SOTP) valuation but is becoming less relevant given their materially higher fire risk compared to Sempra Energy. Furthermore, Smith expects Sempra Energy's Texas capex plan to stay in place despite the opposition to transmission and data centers, though delays to 765-kV projects are likely. While a full recovery for SRE stock will need a clearer outcome from the Texas legislative session, Smith believes that the stock may already be an early opportunity for patient investors.

events.title: NFL and midterm elections set up prediction markets for a critical fall season
events.summary: Prediction market platforms saw volumes grow after two earlier events: the presidential election in 2024, and the start of the NFL season in 2025. The current NFL season opened on Wednesday night, and midterm election campaigns historically kick into high gear after Labor Day. The two dominant incumbents, Polymarket and Kalshi, are working to capitalize off of the two events, as are smaller exchanges that are seeking their slice of the growing market. Prediction markets that rode politics and sports to new heights the past two years are betting on their convergence this autumn to drive even more adoption. In 2024, event contract exchanges entered the mainstream with trades tied to the presidential election that year. Then, in September 2025, the start of the NFL season a year ago marked the beginning of a surge in prediction market trading volume that has yet to slow down. Prediction markets began another NFL season on Wednesday night , when the New England Patriots and Seattle Seahawks dueled it out in a rematch of the 2026 Super Bowl. Labor Day also marked what political observers always consider the start of the midterm election campaign season . This year, prediction markets enter the fall bigger than they've ever been, with daily notional trading volume now consistently in the billions , two dominant incumbents and a host of smaller exchanges chasing them to take some share of the market. And now the two events that separately brought prediction markets mainstream, are happening together over just a few months. "You have a bit of a supercycle occurring right now within the prediction markets," said Robinhood's general manager for futures and prediction markets, JB Mackenzie. Other events are in the wings this season, too, with traders showing greater interest in economic contracts linked to where a hard-to-read Federal Reserve may take interest rates next week, and Major League Baseball playoffs in full swing in October. Prediction platforms have rushed to prepare for the fall's events. That will continue so long as the markets continue to get the majority of their volume from sports offerings, said Seni Thomas, CEO at EDGE Markets , a financial technology company working in sports betting and prediction markets. This season could prove crucial, especially for newer platforms. "This NFL cycle is the real key, make or break" for many newer companies, Thomas said. On Tuesday, Polymarket debuted an advertisement featuring basketball icon LeBron James, former New York Giants quarterback Eli Manning and former Yankee Derek Jeter as part of a football season marketing campaign. It also unveiled a new product for its U.S. exchange which allows users to talk, share and trade together on the platform. Kalshi experienced a record $2.3 billion in volume traded on Saturday, the first day of college football, and unveiled a feature for speculators who participated in 2025 NFL season markets to track how they performed before this season's kickoff. It has also expanded partnerships with individual sports teams ahead of the MLB playoff season. Both platforms suffered glitches as college football play began. Polymarket's U.S. platform was down much of Saturday, and any account that experienced losses due to the outage was eventually refunded. Kalshi prematurely resolved a market on the University of Michigan game, paying traders as if the underdog Western Michigan had pulled off an upset. Later, Kalshi corrected the Michigan result and paid out accordingly. The platforms are leaning into sports, even while battling in court with states across the country that say sports-related event contracts amount to gambling and should fall under their regulatory purview rather than the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, a Wall Street watchdog . "We operate pursuant to the regulations of the CFTC, and we'll continue to do so, and continue to work with stakeholders to run a safe and trusted product," said Ari Borod, president of sports business development at Polymarket in August before announcing a partnership with the New York Yankees. While the two largest prediction market platforms seek to build on their previous NFL success, others are also trying to capitalize on the same sporting events. Rothera , a prediction market platform developed in a joint venture between Susquehanna International Group and Robinhood, is one of them. It saw volumes boom after going online in time for the FIFA World Cup over the summer. "Rolling out all these sports, that's a big lift," CEO Thomas Chippas said. "We've only been live since the last week of May ... We're going as fast as we can, as prudently we can." Novig , a platform that only lists sports event contracts, started an NFL marketing campaign on Wednesday with an ad featuring actress Sydney Sweeney, one of the first celebrities to work with a smaller exchange.

events.title: A dignified life is a ‘distant dream’ for many Iranian families amid US war
events.summary: With constant degradation and no real prospects of improvement in the foreseeable future, people in Iran are losing hope. Tehran, Iran – Iranians born in the 1980s have often considered themselves to be the “burned generation”, living in a period marked by the political and economic turbulence that followed Iran’s 1979 Islamic revolution. The United States embassy hostage crisis , when Iranian activists in 1979 detained American diplomats and others for 444 days, set the tone for a decade ahead. What followed in the 1980s was eight years of gruelling war with neighbouring Iraq, a cultural revolution undertaken by the nascent Islamic Republic, the executions of political prisoners, sanctions and economic uncertainty. Bardia, a 23-year-old living with his parents in eastern Tehran, said many people his age feel they have it even worse than the 1980s generation, due to worsening sanctions creating an even more volatile job market and inflation. “Becoming independent or forming a family, emigrating away, buying a home, a shop, a car or even a new phone is becoming more of a distant dream every day,” he told Al Jazeera, asking to remain anonymous due to security concerns. Decades of domestic mismanagement and corruption paired with external intervention have made life difficult for most of the about 90 million Iranians, even before the US and Israeli war on the country began on February 28. Months of US bombing, intensified sanctions, and naval blockades have significantly worsened the situation this year, in addition to the January antigovernment protests and state-sanctioned restrictions on internet use by the population. Last week, the government hiked petrol prices, which will likely have an inflationary effect, with a feeling that the situation will get worse before it gets better. For people like Bardia, who works at a cafe in downtown Tehran while studying for a business administration degree, it is difficult just to get by. Bardia’s pensioner father is working with online ride-hailing apps and using a 15-year-old low-quality Iranian car to make some money. His mother is a retired garment worker who makes intermittent earnings from sewing at home. After accounting for government cash subsidies and food assistance, the family have about 800 million rials (about $350 at the current exchange rate) per month, while expenses are surging by the day. “We buy meat maybe once every six to eight weeks,” Bardia said. They can no longer afford to eat out or get takeaway, buy new clothes or household appliances, and are hoping that their medical bill does not upend their household budget. By late August, year-on-year inflation was at 89 percent, while food inflation stood at more than 127 percent compared with the same month last year, according to the latest figures released by the Statistical Center of Iran. Iran’s national currency has also continued on a downward spiral, hitting a new all-time low of more than 1.37 million rials per US dollar in Tehran’s open market last week. The rate slightly improved to about 1.31 million on Sunday, after Iranian media said an understanding with Oman over facilitating limited transit through the Strait of Hormuz might materialise before planned talks with regional states in Oman on Monday. But Iran still insists that negotiations with the US will not happen until Tehran’s conditions for Hormuz, lifting the blockade, the sanctions and other demands are met. In the meantime, a maritime blockade has halted most Iranian oil exports, while US sanctions and regional tensions have blocked or hampered air, overland and rail routes, making life difficult for Iranians. “I remember the day my dad bought a car with 10 million tomans [100 million rials – currently worth just $43]. I also remember the day my dad bought a piece of land with 10 million tomans. Today he came home with a little bit of meat and said it was 10 million tomans. I’m in shock; I’m just 24 and I’ve seen all of this!” one Iranian user wrote on X. The number of Iranians posting videos online about the exorbitant amounts they paid for small quantities of food and other essentials has gone viral in recent weeks. But instead of complaining, they, likely ironically, claimed they were happy, because authorities might imprison or execute them if they protested. Last week, a state television report said such videos were “a new project” of dissent by those wishing to overthrow the Islamic Republic by instigating “riots”. After decades of pressure, the economy has shown immense resilience in the face of political upheaval, sanctions, currency fluctuations, and the deadliest COVID-19 pandemic of the Middle East. In less than a year, Iranians have lived through energy crises and two wars started by the US and Israel.

events.title: The US military is preparing for mass casualties in a major war. Its dentists say it's overlooking toothaches.
events.summary: An Air Force dental assistant uses a mobile battlefield dental cleaning machine at Peterson Space Force Base, Colorado., on Aug. 7, 2026. Gino Mattorano/Evans Army Community Hospital Army dentists say war games omit dental emergencies that could strain wartime casualty evacuation. Broken equipment and limited supplies can hinder field dental training opportunities. Forward dental teams can treat patients quickly and return them to duty. A painful toothache or an oral infection might not sound like an injury that could sideline a soldier in combat, but US Army dental leaders warn that in a future conflict, such easily overlooked conditions could take troops out of the fight, consume scarce evacuation capacity, and further stress a strained medical system. Most of the Army's major exercises don't include dental emergencies in their casualty scenarios, dentists said in a recent professional article , leaving commanders with an incomplete picture of the medical and triage or evacuation demands they could face in large-scale combat. Dental emergencies can quickly render troops "non-mission-capable," the authors wrote, because pain can make it difficult to eat, think clearly, or carry out important tasks like operating weapons. They described this as a significant "hidden casualty load." Unlike combat wounds, most dental problems can be easily fixed if dental teams are nearby, but despite their important role in military health care, "deployable dental capabilities continue to decline," authors wrote, underscoring an "urgent need for accurate dental emergency modeling in war-gaming to emphasize the importance of [non-battle related injuries] and dental emergencies." Past wars indicate substantial demand. Dental emergencies accounted for 19% of all treatment at military hospitals near the front lines during the war in Iraq. Another recent article by Army dentists said that dental disease and other non-battle injuries made up nearly 16% of all medical evacuations among troops fighting the Islamic State in Iraq and Syria. Almost all dental patients treated by forward dental teams returned to duty after one or two visits, the authors wrote. Without dental care close to the front, however, soldiers may have to travel farther to receive treatment, potentially removing them from duty for as long as a week. Casualty evacuations for any type of health concern or injury, major or minor, are likely to pose a problem for the military in future large-scale combat. The proliferation of drones, both attack and surveillance systems, across the Ukrainian battlefield have made quick evacuation largely impossible, a stark difference from the US experience during the post-9/11 wars. In a recent military news release for a healthcare training event, Army dentist Lt. Col. Jesse Thietten said dental care "is a low-hanging-fruit solution for medical as a whole. Military medicine needs solutions to account for the anticipated systemic medical overload in [large-scale conflicts.]" Dental emergencies could rank among the top five most common reasons for casualty evacuation in such a fight, Thietten added. For troops deployed abroad in multinational settings alongside partner forces, dental concerns are "the number one reason" for casualty evacuation, he added. Thietten helped develop a lightweight expeditionary dental platform for special operations teams training in remote parts of Europe, where teams asked for help treating dental emergencies without easy access to traditionally robust medical facilities. The goal was to bring care closer to troops rather than having to shuttle them to far-off clinics. Such an approach reflects what Thietten argues the broader force will need in a future fight, including more dental work before troops deploy, along with smaller, more mobile dental teams that can operate close to units in the field. Within the Air Force, less than 1% of the service's dentists deploy," said Air Force Col. Anita Shade, chief of dental services for the 21st Medical Group, in the same news release. "Our dental teams are often disconnected from the heart of the readiness mission that we work to support, day in and day out," she said. That disconnect may become more pronounced when combat casualties can't easily be moved from the battlefield to established hospitals and care facilities. "Asymmetric/hybrid drone warfare shows us that we now need to plan and prepare for prolonged patient management in the field due to the unpredictability of patient transport," Shade said. Another problem for some military dentists is more basic — broken field equipment and a lack of medical supplies, hampering training opportunities. Two Army dentists cited those problems in another article from this summer on how military dentistry must adapt for future conflict. While preparing for a unit exercise, they found that their field equipment had not been used in nearly a year and that critical equipment including their sterilizer unit was broken, underscoring further readiness challenges. events.title: We organized the National Civics Bee — it’s where to start if you want better workers
events.summary: Students are heading back to school in the 250th year since our nation’s founding. Unfortunately, many of them may not be aware of what the nation’s founding entailed, as only 22% of eighth-graders in this country are proficient in civics according to the  most recent National Assessment of Educational Progress .  These students are aware, however, that the world around them is changing, and that AI will have a profound impact on what they need to know to succeed when they leave the classroom. Asked this month which skills will matter most as artificial intelligence reshapes work, teenagers surveyed by Common Sense Media pointed to working well with others, fact-checking and critical thinking, and making sense of complicated information. Employers have been saying much the same thing for years, with only 18% of business leaders believing entry-level hires are ready for today’s workplace. We tend to treat these as separate worries, one about the health of our democracy and the other about the strength of our workforce. But they actually have more in common than one might think, and there’s a strong case to be made that improving civics knowledge would go a long way toward building the skills students and employers are seeking.  As our nation invests heavily in career pathways, credentials, artificial intelligence, and technical training, we must also invest in one of our country’s most overlooked drivers of workforce readiness: high-quality civic learning. As the organizers and researchers of the National Civics Bee—a nationwide, nonpartisan civics competition for middle school students—we’ve witnessed firsthand how civic learning can also help students develop the skills employers and students want. This year, more than 20,000 students are participating through over 240 local chambers of commerce and community partners across all 50 states, Washington, D.C., and American Samoa. Students gain civic knowledge and put it to use by identifying issues they see in their communities, researching those concerns from multiple perspectives, developing potential solutions, and discussing their ideas before judges. In post-competition surveys, 98% of participants identified at least one meaningful benefit from the experience. Nearly three-quarters improved their writing. Many reported greater confidence discussing public issues, a stronger understanding of local government, and more frequent conversations about civic issues at home. Three-quarters said they felt prepared to defend a position on a controversial issue respectfully and thoughtfully. Consider Emily Brubaker. Born with a rare medical condition that created significant challenges for her family, she entered the National Civics Bee determined to explore a public policy issue that had personally affected her. She researched the topic, built support for her ideas, and traveled to Washington, D.C. to meet with lawmakers to discuss potential solutions. In the process, she practiced many of the same skills employers value in the workplace: research, communication, collaboration, persistence, and the ability to turn challenges into solutions. Not every middle school student will lobby Congress, but civic learning gives young people opportunities to tackle authentic challenges before anyone is paying them to do so. Experiences like the Bee help students develop the very qualities employers consistently say they need most. Unfortunately, few young people are given meaningful opportunities to engage with real issues in school, where they can practice and hone skills before entering the real world.  Our nation’s founders saw a citizenry educated in its liberties as a precondition for the republic—a sentiment echoed by Horace Mann half a century later when, as the first Secretary of the Massachusetts Board of Education, he identified civic education—what he called political education—as a core pillar of a public education system. That sentiment persisted into the 1960s, with high schools commonly requiring three courses in civics and government. Over time, however, civics has been crowded out by competing academic priorities. Today, most states require just one civics course—and often only a semester—and opportunities to put civic skills into practice are limited: just one-third of high schools offer debate teams, one-quarter offer mock trials, and a mere 20% offer mock elections. Civics instruction is equally lacking in younger grades. A 2022 report from the RAND Corp. on K-5 social studies called out a “ missing infrastructure ,” referring to the gaps in policies, resources, and required testing that encourage classroom instruction on civics. These gaps are not accidental. They reflect where we put our money. Federal investment in STEM education runs roughly $50 per student each year, while civic education receives  less than fifty cents  per student. That is troubling for democracy, but it should also worry employers. If students are not learning how institutions work, how decisions get made, how to evaluate competing claims, or how to participate constructively in public discourse, we should not be surprised when they struggle to navigate increasingly complex workplaces. Technical expertise has never been enough, which is why businesses already invest billions of dollars each year in onboarding, leadership development, and professional training. What if future employees arrived on their first day having already practiced these capabilities for years in classrooms, communities, and civic life? The National Civics Bee is just one example of what becomes possible when civic learning is treated as an investment rather than an afterthought. As America begins its next 250 years, employers should not wait for the talent pipeline to fix itself. If we want a workforce capable of adapting to change, navigating complexity, and strengthening our communities, those capacities must be cultivated early.  The next generation of leaders, workers, and citizens is sitting in a middle school classroom right now. It’s time to invest accordingly. The opinions expressed in Fortune.com commentary pieces are solely the views of their authors and do not necessarily reflect the opinions and beliefs of Fortune .
