events.title: Gloria Steinem opened the door. Now women need a seat at the table
events.summary: When David Grinberg’s 22-year-old daughter, Ily, started her career in wealth management in Chicago this summer, he was thrilled. But as an M&A attorney at Sidley Austin who has spent years advising entrepreneurs — and as the father of three daughters — he noticed something else: Ily was usually the only woman in the room. Then, just a couple months into the job, Ily was asked to present part of a proposed wealth plan to a real client. She nailed it and received terrific feedback from her team. For David, it was a small but important moment. Because what he wants for his daughters isn’t complicated: the opportunity to do whatever they are capable of doing, without being held back because they are women. But he also knows ability alone isn’t always enough. David, who also serves on Girls With Impact’s Los Angeles board, represents founders and family-owned businesses, many in the beauty and wellness industry and many led by women. He has watched extraordinarily successful female entrepreneurs build companies worth hundreds of millions of dollars — and still encounter people who second-guess their judgment. He has seen how important it can be for women entering male-dominated fields to have other women around them: as mentors, sounding boards and examples of what is possible. When I asked him what young women need most to navigate that world, he came back to one word: confidence. “The younger someone can start learning skills, the sooner they will understand what they can accomplish and the better they will be,” he told me. Confidence, he believes, comes from doing something successfully and realizing: I can do that. Then carrying that belief into the next challenge. His comments stayed with me because they came just as America lost Gloria Steinem. “We’re at the end of an era of unprecedented progress for women,” Lorraine Hariton, former CEO of Catalyst, told me as we discussed Steinem’s passing. But, she added, “these are fragile times and we still have an unfinished agenda. It’s time to pass the baton to a new generation.” That is precisely where we are. Steinem’s generation fought to open doors that had been closed to women for generations. Our challenge now isn’t simply keeping those doors open. It is preparing the next generation of women to walk through them with the confidence to speak up, take their seats at the table—and eventually lead the organizations behind them. The baton is being passed. But America still has a long way to go. The World Economic Forum estimates that global gender parity remains more than a century away . The U.S. ranks 42nd globally, with significant gaps remaining in economic and political leadership. I’ve spent much of my career on the other side of the doors Gloria Steinem’s generation helped open. Today, I spend my time preparing young women to walk through them. And what I see makes me both optimistic and impatient. Women hold nearly half (47%) of entry-level jobs in America. They earn nearly 60%   of bachelor’s degrees, build companies, support families and enter professions once largely closed to them. And don’t mistake the popularity of the “trad wife” on social media for the aspirations of an entire generation. The young women I meet want choices. They want careers, financial independence and the opportunity to reach their full economic potential. Yet economic participation is not the same as economic power. Women are nearly half of America’s workforce, yet hold just 31% of senior leadership positions. The disparity is even more striking for entrepreneurs. Of roughly $265 billion in U.S. venture capital invested in 2025, just 1.2% went to companies with all-female founding teams. Half the talent cannot remain a fraction of the leadership and capital if America expects to compete at its best. David sees this from both ends of the pipeline. His daughter is just beginning her career. Many of the female founders he represents have already built enormously successful businesses. Yet even at that level, he has seen women encounter senior executives or investors who assume they know better than the woman who actually built the company. He has also seen the opposite: women supporting other women because they understand that every woman who succeeds makes it easier for the next generation to envision herself doing the same. “So often, you’re influenced by what you see,” he told me. That’s why having more women at the table matters. Not simply for representation, but because who young women see leading helps shape what they believe is possible for themselves. And these disparities don’t suddenly appear in the C-suite. Girls begin questioning their abilities at age 6. By 14 , their confidence has dropped 30%. Recruiters tell me they see talented young women enter job interviews less likely to speak up and advocate for themselves—behaviors that can affect everything from their first job to their lifetime earnings. The irony? Research shows women outperform men on 17 of 19 leadership capabilities. Yet too many young women still resist calling themselves leaders. That is why the next chapter of women’s advancement must start earlier. We need to equip girls with confidence, business skills, networks, financial knowledge and technological fluency before they enter the workplace. We need to give them opportunities to try, fail, succeed and discover that they can do hard things. We need classrooms where girls’ ideas are taken seriously and workplaces where young women can see a path to leadership. AI makes this work even more urgent. The workplace is being reconstructed before our eyes. Entry-level jobs and traditional career ladders are changing. Employers increasingly expect AI proficiency from new hires. If young women aren’t deliberately prepared for this new economy, yesterday’s victories will not guarantee tomorrow’s opportunities. And this isn’t simply a women’s issue. It’s an American competitiveness issue. When women gain greater economic power, the benefits ripple outward. Research shows they invest disproportionately in their families — strengthening financial resilience, communities, and the pipeline of future leaders and entrepreneurs. Imagine what America could achieve if we fully developed the economic potential of half our population. At a time when global competitiveness increasingly depends on talent, innovation and leadership, we cannot afford to leave that potential on the sidelines. Gloria Steinem’s generation fought so women could have choices their mothers and grandmothers never had. Our responsibility isn’t simply to admire what they accomplished. It is to build on it. If there is one message to take from Steinem’s passing, perhaps it is this: We cannot wait for the next generation of leaders to emerge. We have to create the conditions for them to become leaders. The baton has been passed. What we do with it now is up to us. The opinions expressed in Fortune.com commentary pieces are solely the views of

events.title: I run an organization dedicated to collective grieving. I recognize a familiar dynamic with AI in the workplace
events.summary: When someone we love dies, we understand why grief hurts: someone mattered, and their absence reshapes our world. Mourning allows us to honor what was, mark what ended, and listen for what our grief reveals about what we value. That recognition can guide what we carry forward. Death, however, is not the only loss humans grieve. While technological rupture differs from bereavement, the rapid, widespread adoption of AI is setting the stage for a psychological crisis of grief across corporate America. In boardrooms and breakrooms alike, employees are silently grappling with unprecedented new anxieties: What becomes of the skills I spent years mastering? Have I lost confidence in my colleagues when I question whether AI is responsible for their work? Am I myself losing the muscle to think critically without AI? Will my function become obsolete? Behind these questions are several forms of grief—a mourning of lost professional identities, eroded trust, and envisioned career paths that are vanishing overnight. As the co-founder and executive director of Reimagine , an organization dedicated to helping individuals and communities navigate grief collectively, I recognize a deeply familiar dynamic unfolding in today’s AI-driven workplace. Whenever human beings face fundamental loss, whether personal or systemic, a common instinct is to try to turn away from it or suppress it. But if we don’t integrate our grief in healthy ways, it has negative consequences for our physical and mental health, and it can often lead to destructive action. Recent corporate data confirms that this tension is already fracturing company cultures. An August 2026 Gallup study revealed that employees at organizations deploying AI extensively were significantly more likely to report a worsening workplace culture. Meanwhile, Microsoft’s Work Trend Index found that 53% of workers worried that relying on AI for critical tasks made them look replaceable, while over half admitted to hiding their AI usage from management entirely. When leaders fail to acknowledge the rising grief, or actively dismiss it as standard “employee resistance to change,” they miss the core issue. Failure to address these non-death workplace losses carries severe organizational costs. Reimagine’s own recent research , conducted in partnership with HarrisX, explores the realities of U.S. adults’ experience with non-death loss. The findings show that when major disruptions go unsupported by others, they lead to experiences of distress comparable to grief from death loss. The reported consequences include high levels of isolation, anger toward others, distrust of institutions, and physical symptoms such as sleep problems, fatigue, pain, or illness—comparable to those reported by people grieving a death.. To lead effectively through the AI transition, executives should move beyond forced optimism and make room for employees to name what they fear losing. By listening to what people grieve, leaders can identify the values at risk and find new ways to live them forward as work changes. The answers can lead to practical choices. Grief over lost mastery might lead organizations to invest more deeply in mentorship and hands-on learning. Grief over eroding trust might prompt clearer norms around authorship, honesty, and transparency—and, in turn, a more candid, connected workplace. Grief over low-quality, AI-generated work may reveal just how much we value quality, care, and human judgment.  When leaders first acknowledge that the grief is real and then take steps like these to honor what is being lost, employees can feel seen in their grief rather than misunderstood, as though they are failing or becoming obsolete.  Listening to employees does not mean stopping progress, nor does it absolve employers of responsibility. Workers are still owed transparency, meaningful transition support, and a real voice in decisions that affect their futures; thoughtful recognition should not be designed to secure acceptance of decisions already made. Our task is not simply to process what AI takes and move on. It is to name what we are losing, listen for the values our grief reveals, and give them new form. That is how grief can restore agency at work: not by returning work to what it was, but by helping us shape what comes next. events.title: Security through obscurity is dead, and AI delivered the fatal blow
events.summary: The term "security through obscurity" describes an old idea that networks and systems will remain secure so long as their architecture, along with any vulnerabilities or other weaknesses, remains secret or hidden. It was never a sound strategy for protecting sensitive assets and systems, but many organizations leaned on it due to lack of resources or complacency. Now it’s obsolete. Don’t believe us? Here’s proof. Software vendors and independent researchers alike are now using AI agents to find bugs – some very obscure and decades old – across products and open source code, leading to record-breaking numbers of security disclosures and patches, and a massive backlog for project maintainers. “You see open source platforms that have been visible to the tech community for a decade, these libraries that are run in 80 percent of web servers out there, people have stress-tested those for 10 years, and the community believed that they were really secure,” Brett Leatherman, assistant director of the FBI's Cyber Division, told The Register. “The latest models were able to break those and say, ‘yeah, there’s significant vulnerabilities in here.’” Whether or not security through obscurity is dead “isn't even an opinion question,” Trend Micro’s Zero Day Initiative chief bug hunter Dustin Childs told The Register, the day after Microsoft’s record-breaking Patch Tuesday addressed 974 CVEs. “When you look at all of the components patched by Adobe and Microsoft yesterday, you see components no one has talked about in years,” Childs said. “Telnet client – is this even still used in any secure environment? Windows RNDIS – the USB-networking protocol Microsoft has been trying to deprecate for years. NFS Portmapper – 1980s Unix tech. And Link Layer Topology Discovery – the Vista-era network-map protocol nobody's thought about since Vista – just to name a few.” Meanwhile, attackers are also using AI to reverse-engineer fixes and find exploits within hours. In one recent case, at least four espionage crews, most suspected of links to China, slammed shut the “patch-gap” window for open source Chromium, using an exploit kit developed shortly after the maintainers released an upstream patch – but before the downstream stable release was pushed to users. What this means for OT security During interviews at Black Hat in August, both former US National Cyber Director Chris Inglis and John Hultquist, chief analyst at Google Threat Intelligence Group, told us that they worry about what this means for critical operational technologies and industrial control systems (ICS). These are the systems that ensure the lights turn on when people flip a switch, gas flows out of pumps, and safe drinking water pours from faucets – all critical services that people use daily, and assume will continue working reliably. The OT systems themselves often use obscure protocols and proprietary hardware and software, which historically made them black boxes, even to IT specialists and hackers. AI upended this assumption. It means that criminals don't need to be OT experts to carry out destructive cyberattacks on critical networks and facilities. They just have to ask an agent to learn everything about these systems and do the dirty work for them. A couple of weeks after Black Hat, five US agencies said that attackers used AI-generated exploitation scripts to break into internet-exposed Siemens S7 Series programmable logic controllers (PLCs) at water, manufacturing, energy, and other critical facilities. “This is not a theoretical risk – it is an active threat,” the feds warned. AI “is excellent at technical troubleshooting, at knowing obscure systems and helping you make your way through it, and this makes me very concerned about industrial control systems,” Hultquist told The Register in an interview last week. “They've been largely secured because the expertise was in a handful of people's heads, and that's not going to last forever,” he said. AI can be a useful guide for attackers studying not just the application layer, but also the operating system, and even down into the firmware, Hultquist added. “That's going to have implications for a lot of different areas of security, but definitely for industrial control systems.” However, while this undoubtedly means more work for sysadmins and defenders, burying this outdated idea of security through obscurity isn’t necessarily a bad thing. 'Never a winning strategy' “I've always been of the mind that security through obscurity was never a winning strategy,” Katie Moussouris, founder and CEO of bug bounty consultancy Luta Security and the fairy godmother of bug bounties, told The Register. “But that's because I've been a hacker for so long. The argument always fails in the face of someone who decides to turn their gaze towards your organization. If there is something to find, they will find it.” Plus, she added, AI makes hacking a whole lot easier. “People might not have familiarity with the particular tech stack that you're running, but that is no longer a barrier because AI has ingested everything, and an AI is going to help them enumerate weak spots, even if they themselves are not familiar with the particular tech stack that they are pointing an AI towards,” Moussouris said. However, finding bugs and other weaknesses has never been the big security problem, she added. “It’s triaging and prioritization and actually getting things fixed.” This, Moussouris said, has also been her biggest issue with the way that organizations implement bug bounty programs. “AI is shining that bright light on the wrong end of the security picture, and unfortunately, AI hasn't caught up on the defensive side,” Moussouris said. “We're not there with AI automated patching, remediation – anything of the sort.” A couple of recent studies back this up, both finding that AI-generated patches fail more than half of the time. 1Password’s research team took six CVEs disclosed since March, and produced 6,080 patches using two frontier models: OpenAI's ChatGPT-5.5 and Anthropic's Opus 4.8. “The average success rate for generating a patch that fully resolved the vulnerability (without materially changing application behavior) was just 26.0 percent,” wrote Director of Security Research Keith Hoodlet, adding that even patches that did fix the flaw also mucked up the application’s behavior 20 percent of the time. This included things like changing “allow list” logic to “deny list” logic. “Conversely, LLM-generated patches did not resolve the vulnerability, added a new vulnerability, or both, an average 53.9% of the time,” Hoodlet said. Another study by app security shop Veracode found that, across more than 100 models and 80 coding tasks, the average security pass rate for AI-generated code was just 56 percent. “If people are telling you that you need to accelerate on the fixing side, and the defense side – that’s just not cutting it,” Moussouris said. “Orgs that are looking at this as we're going to throw

events.title: Virgin Group CEO scrolls TikTok daily to keep up with Gen Z: ‘The zeitgeist is not with people in their 50s’
events.summary: As Gen Z finds itself increasingly consumed by social media algorithms and doomscolling , they’re not the only ones glued to their feeds. Increasingly, Gen X CEOs are scrolling right alongside them. Virgin Group CEO Josh Bayliss regularly turns to TikTok —not simply for a mid-afternoon dopamine hit, but to better understand how younger generations think, what they care about, and where new business opportunities may be emerging. “The zeitgeist is not people in their 50s like me,” Bayliss, 53, told Fortune . “The zeitgeist is 20-something year olds who are shaping the culture that we have an obligation to serve.” But unlike CEOs like McDonald’s Chris Kempczinski or Costco’s Ron Vachris , who have frequently appeared on their companies’ social media accounts, Bayliss isn’t trying to make himself part of the content. Instead, he simply sees keeping up with trends as a viewer as an increasingly essential part of his job. With more than 49.5 million Gen Zers on TikTok alone, viral moments can reshape consumer behavior overnight. And as the leader of a conglomerate spanning an airline, gym chain, hotel group, telecommunications giant, and commercial space-tourism business, Bayliss said he can’t afford to lose sight of what younger consumers care about. “The way that Gen Z or millennials think about social justice, think about equality, think about inclusion, think about environmental issues—they are our target audience, and that’s where we have an obligation, I think, to listen all the time,” Bayliss said. For brands, it’s also a way to interact directly with consumers and get ahead of trends that could make or break their business models. “You’ve got to have the volume turned up 24/7, honestly,” Bayliss added. Keeping up with younger consumers is getting harder—and more important Staying up to date with younger consumers is hardly a new business imperative. But as technology and culture move faster, executives face a growing pressure to understand what’s happening around them—before they have to rely on a younger employee to explain it. “Audiences want to interact with brands that are socially aware and respectful in their messaging,” wrote Evan Kropp, an instructor at the University of Florida’s College of Journalism and Communications. “This goes beyond using trending hashtags. It means hiring diverse creators, listening to feedback, and staying informed about social and cultural conversations.”  That’s one reason brands increasingly aren’t just posting on social media—they’re inserting themselves into the conversations already happening there by commenting on viral videos and engaging with users directly. Virgin’s social media team, for example , frequently responds to comments on its own posts, embracing the idea that brands need to let consumers know they are listening—rather than simply broadcasting messages to them. “Companies that embrace cultural fluency can build stronger communities and deepen brand loyalty,” Kropp added. “It also helps them avoid costly missteps in public perception.” Lifelong learning is a constant part of leadership, CEOs say Virgin’s founder Richard Branson has long embraced the power of brand development. The 76-year-old has built a substantial social media presence, with more than 4.9 million followers on Instagram alone. But, he has also repeatedly emphasized he doesn’t know everything—and thus it is important to stay curious and learn throughout one’s career.   “As someone who didn’t finish school, I think it’s so important to become a lifelong learner and embrace an endless curiosity about the world,” Branson wrote in 2019.  Indra Nooyi , the former CEO of PepsiCo , has similarly argued reaching the top of a company doesn’t mean learning stops. If anything, she said, it’s when the difficult part begins. “When you become a CEO, the game just begins,” she said at an Amazon tech conference in 2025. “The tough life just begins, okay? If you think you’ve landed, you’re mistaken.” AT&T CEO John Stankey has recently taken a more structured approach to the same idea. The Fortune 500 executive said he frequently seeks a “reverse mentor”—someone younger who can help him understand how younger generations think and use technology.  “My kids aren’t in the house anymore, so I need a little bit more time with people in their 20s than what I used to have,” Stankey said in a recent joint interview with JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon hosted by LinkedIn . “I like to listen to what they’re doing and what’s important in their life and how they’re using technology.” Stankey also has a system for the moments when he encounters something he doesn’t understand in a meeting, whether it’s a new trend, software or piece of Gen Z lingo. “I’ll go into some meetings and somebody will say something, I’ll go, ‘What the heck is that? What are they talking about?’” Stankey said. Rather than slow down the meeting to ask—he said he just “pretends” he knows what it is—and then jots it down on a notecard. “I pull the card out at night right before I go to sleep, and I go on the internet,” he said. “Now I go and I have a conversation with my chatbot to educate me a little bit about what that subject is, and so just being disciplined about how you learn is really really critical.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Xi says China will take lead to foster AI, tech cooperation among BRICS countries
events.summary: China will take the lead to help foster artificial-intelligence collaboration and development among developing-economy countries, President Xi Jinping said at the BRICS bloc summit in New Delhi. The country will also work to establish a BRICS digital ecosystem cloud platform, and conduct digital skills training, technological exchange and industrial alignment, Xi said. He also proposed setup of a BRICS engineer cultivation alliance and a youth exchange program for scientific and technological innovation. China will take the lead to help foster artificial-intelligence collaboration and development among developing countries, President Xi Jinping said at the BRICS bloc summit in New Delhi. China will pioneer the establishment of a BRICS AI open-source community, support the cooperation in developing and applying large language models, hold AI seminars and training courses, and build an open AI ecosystem, Xi said in a statement on Sunday released by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The country will also work to establish a BRICS digital ecosystem cloud platform, and conduct digital skills training, technological exchange and industrial alignment, Xi said. He also proposed setup of a BRICS engineer cultivation alliance and a youth exchange program for scientific and technological innovation. XI's proposals come as the AI sector booms, with companies releasing ever-more-powerful models at a frenetic pace. AI itself has come under scrutiny too, with one researcher who worked at both OpenAI and Anthropic this week saying that many people working in the industry believe AI might kill all of humanity by the end of the decade. Xi didn't address the ongoing debate about AI safety. BRICS was established in 2009 as a counterweight to Western dominance and originally comprised ​Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa. It eventually grew to include Egypt, Ethiopia, ​Indonesia, Iran and the United Arab Emirates.

events.title: AI staff 'genuinely frightened' for humanity's future, ex-Anthropic researcher tells BBC
events.summary: 'There is a possibility of human extinction,' former Anthropic employee says about AI Published 13 September 2026, 02:15 BST An artificial intelligence researcher who quit AI firm Anthropic has said people working on the technology were "genuinely frightened" about the speed of its advancements and what it could mean for humanity. "I believe that if we don't slow down at the current rate of progress, there is a strong chance that we could all die in the immediate future," he said. Jacob Coxon was speaking to the BBC after his resignation post on the dangers of AI went viral on a backdrop of growing safety concerns about the industry. The 27-year-old's former boss, Anthropic head Dario Amodei, recently called for AI development to slow down - though some have questioned the motivations behind this. The bosses of two rival AI firms, Sam Altman of OpenAI and Elon Musk of xAI, have both said they agree with Amodei's proposal for industry-wide deceleration and regulation, as well as independent monitoring of AI model development. Amodei wrote in an essay on Saturday that developing the technology was not in question, but the risks associated with it were "serious", and that companies and governments must be given time to address them. Coxon – who worked at OpenAI before joining Anthropic – welcomed the suggestion of a slowdown but said it would need to be co-ordinated with China to avoid "a race at an international scale". "The people who work at these companies are completely serious when they ask for regulation because they find themselves trapped in a race. And they're scared of the outcomes of that race," he told Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg. Anthropic boss Dario Amodei calls for AI development to slow down Published 16 hours ago The hardest question to answer, according to Coxon, was what an AI apocalypse would look like. One of the risks outlined in Amodei's comments was of a swarm of bots acting like a supercomputer that could take over the internet. Coxon said this scenario could be realistic in six months to a year. In response to Coxon's departure, an Anthropic spokesperson told BBC News: "We have always been transparent that AI will bring both enormous benefits and unprecedented risks. "To address these risks, we continue to build models with some of the strongest safeguards in the industry." The firm has been a pioneer in studying how AI models work, the spokesperson added. It was the first to publish a framework for mitigating the risks posed by their development - and it also "aggressively" tests its models and publishes the findings to aid scrutiny and prevent incidents of "AI misalignment". "This work is also why we believe the world would benefit from the industry adopting a lawful, verifiable way to work together to pace how we release powerful models," they said. Coxon said his peers feared the danger could even arrive in the next two years. He said staff at AI firms were "planning what to do with their lives and thinking about the impacts of their work", while some were "considering buying land somewhere because they're so scared of the instability as a result of rapid AI progress". "They all keep this in their head on a daily basis while working on the technology." But Coxon did have some optimism about the future of AI, telling the BBC that the people researching the technology "genuinely want to see the upside" of things like "solving diseases and improving everyone's lives". Anthropic researcher believes more than 10% chance AI 'could kill all humans' Published 3 days ago Many others in the industry have also voiced their concerns since Coxon's social media post, including Anthropic scientist Evan Hubinger . "We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans! I personally think it is >10% within the next decade," Hubinger said. Computer scientist and Nobel Prize winner Geoffrey Hinton, known as the "Godfather of AI", told the BBC on Friday that a 10% chance of AI killing all humans was "not unreasonable" , external . Meanwhile, Marc Warner, chief executive of AI safety firm Faculty, told the BBC's The World This Weekend that it was "extremely hard to place a probability" on AI killing all humans. "But it's important to recognise that these people are very sincere in what they're saying," he added, noting that the risks surrounding AI have been raised by the heads of several AI firms for years. Former Prime Minister Rishi Sunak, who is a paid adviser to Anthropic, wrote in the Sunday Times , external that he too was worried about the risk of AI to humanity despite generally being optimistic. Dramatic insider warnings over AI fall flat with some in Silicon Valley Published 5 hours ago However, some industry figures have suggested comments about the perils and power of AI may be designed to generate hype.

events.title: The tab is coming due for America's borrowing binge
events.summary: Americans are facing a rising tab as a multi-decade borrowing binge collides with a spike in energy prices caused by the Iran war. The big picture: Long-term interest rates are surging, as are consumer prices. It's a toxic mix of near-term inflation pressures and years of fiscal imbalance. Driving the news: The yield on the benchmark 10-year U.S. Treasury note rose to 4.97% Friday, up a full percentage point since the end of February, and only a hair below its high since 2007. The rate on a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage has risen in lockstep, reaching 7.08% Friday, per Mortgage News Daily — the highest in more than a year. State of play: The immediate catalyst Friday was an inflation report that showed consumer prices surging higher in August, with gasoline prices accounting for more than a third of the gain. Gasoline is now at a national average of $4.29 a gallon, while the price of diesel has climbed to over $6 a gallon. All this means that the Federal Reserve is now expected to raise its target interest rate this week. But longer-term borrowing rates are set in global markets — and determined by bigger forces. The U.S. government is spending about $2 trillion a year more than it raises in taxes at a time the cumulative debt is already roughly 100% of a year's GDP. Long-term bond yields have been rising worldwide, reflecting both high government borrowing and demand for capital from the AI buildout. The intrigue: The recent spikes have taken place in spite of interventions by Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent to try to smooth turbulent bond markets — efforts that haven't succeeded in making borrowing cheaper. And rather than focus on the deficit reduction the bond market wants, President Trump has floated the notion of $5,000 payments to all U.S. adult citizens if Republicans win midterm elections. The U.S. government is already spending around $1 trillion a year in interest on the debt, on track to rise to $2 trillion over the next decade, a new high as a share of the economy. If the recent surge in rates is sustained, those numbers will grow even higher. The bottom line: The combination of near-term energy-driven inflation and the long-term debt trajectory means that it will cost more to borrow money for the foreseeable future.

events.title: I moved away from my home country 6 years ago. When I returned, I felt like an outsider.
events.summary: The author moved from Mexico to the US and then to the UK. Courtesy of Santiago Barraza Lopez Six years ago, I left my home country, Mexico, and moved to New York, then to the UK. I recently returned to Mexico after a long time away and was surprised by how much it has changed. I felt like an outsider, and realized I had changed even more. I grew up in Mexico City and spent most of my life there. Six years ago, I left the country, first for the US and later for the UK, but I never stopped thinking of my birthplace as the place I ultimately belonged. This summer, I returned after two years away, the longest stretch I had ever gone without visiting home . I expected the trip to feel nostalgic and effortless. Instead, I was surprised by how tiring it felt and, for the first time, how slightly out of place I seemed to be. Mexico City had changed while I was away The first thing that struck me was how different the city itself felt. Mexico City had always been huge, chaotic, and international in its own way, but the version I returned to felt noticeably more cosmopolitan than the one I remembered. There were new restaurants everywhere, more international businesses , more English being spoken around me, and far more foreigners than I remembered seeing before I left. Areas that once felt deeply familiar now seemed to belong to a newer version of the city. I did not necessarily dislike any of it. But it surprised me how quickly I started feeling like someone who had missed a chapter. I was the one asking what had opened, what had closed, where people went now, and which places had become popular. For the first time, I was not the person who knew instinctively how the city worked. That was strange because I had always thought of Mexico City as something fixed in my life. I was the one who had moved away, so part of me had unconsciously expected it to remain roughly as I had left it. The city had changed, but many of the people I knew somehow hadn't Mexico City felt almost unrecognizable in places, but spending time with people I had known for years created the opposite sensation. Despite all the time that had passed, some conversations felt as though I had only been away for a few weeks. On paper, a lot had changed. Friends had gotten married, moved in with partners, started having children, changed jobs , and taken on responsibilities that did not exist when we were younger. Their lives had clearly moved forward. And yet, with certain exceptions, I sometimes found myself listening to the same stories, the same frustrations, and even the same problems I remembered from years earlier. Certain relationship dynamics had barely shifted. People worried about versions of the same things they had worried about before I left. It was a strange feeling. I had expected two years away to make everyone seem dramatically different, particularly because so many of them had crossed major life milestones in that time. Instead, I often recognized not just the people themselves, but the exact patterns I remembered. There was something comforting about that familiarity, but also something disorienting. The city around us seemed to have accelerated, while parts of the social world I had left behind felt almost preserved. That contrast eventually forced me to consider another possibility. Maybe the reason everything felt so different to me was not because everyone else had changed beyond recognition. Maybe I had. I realized the biggest change was me The last two years have probably changed me more than I understood before this trip. My relationship became more serious, and my partner and I started living together, which altered the rhythm of my everyday life in ways that felt gradual at the time but obvious once I stepped away from them. I no longer organize my days entirely around myself. We make plans together, decide how to spend our weekends, travel as a couple , share responsibilities, and build routines around one another. Even the boring parts of life, like deciding what to eat or how to spend a quiet evening, have become part of a shared structure. Being back in Mexico made me notice how attached I had become to that structure. I missed my apartment, my work routine, my evenings with my partner, and even the ordinary habits I would never normally think were worth missing. The things pulling me back were not landmarks or anything particularly British. They were simply the details of the life I had built. That realization helped explain why the trip had felt so tiring and unfamiliar. Mexico was still deeply important to me, and the people I loved there were still part of who I was, but the center of my everyday existence had shifted somewhere else. For years, I thought of myself as someone who lived in London but went home to Mexico. This trip made me realize that London is home now. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Why is the Trump administration calling bike lanes ‘DEI’? | Dave Schilling
events.summary: Why is the Trump administration calling bike lanes ‘DEI’? The government apparently has an issue with paths for cyclists. Take it from someone who can’t ride a bike: this makes no sense I ’m out of gas. Not metaphorically. Literally, my car has the barest minimum amount of fuel in it. This is not because I like to live dangerously , a la the great literary hero Austin Powers, but because gas is more expensive than ever. I have nowhere to be today, so I’m allowing my car to sit idle, empty and alone, lest my bank account disappear into the Phantom Zone of negative balance. If things get sticky, I can take public transit or, God forbid, ride a bike. Except I can’t ride a bike, thanks to my parents, who were too busy doing more important tasks than teaching me, like arguing or falling asleep. But for many Americans, riding a bike is a perfectly normal thing to do. Am I humiliated that one of the many basic skills for life that I don’t know is considered so simple that it became a common idiom for something that’s easy ? Yes, of course. I don’t live dangerously, I live humiliatingly. Humiliation is my middle name. Dave Humiliation Schilling. Go on, point and laugh at the photo of me in this article. Get it out of your system so we can move along. As I was saying, many people can ride a bike if they can’t drive a car for whatever reason, and they’ll be perfectly happy doing it. They smile broadly as the wind whips through the holes in their helmet and gently touches the exposed hairs on their head. They pedal like their lives depend on it (they do), dodging deadly automobiles operated by inattentive drivers. In some cities, there are dedicated lanes for these brave bikers, theoretically inoculating them from the dangers of cars pancaking them. The United States has 4,400 directional miles of bike lanes , offering safety for anyone serious enough to risk it. The push for bike lanes began in the 1960s and grew in the ensuing decades. Theoretically, the lanes offer a carbon-neutral alternative to driving a car. If one chooses to bike instead of drive, it’s one fewer toxin-spewing death trap creating pollution and traffic congestion on the motorways. That sounds like a boon for the world, so naturally, the Trump administration wants to do away with it. Condemning “ DEI bike lanes ”, the Trump administration has made a point of freezing or canceling related grants, referring to alternative transit options as unworkable in the United States, and suggesting removing the lanes that already exist. Their logic, if we are using that term loosely, is that bike lanes take space away from cars, create more traffic, and lead to chaotic roads. I suppose that’s true, if we assume that there is an infinite number of cars and bikes are just extra, rather than an alternative that takes cars off the street. But that clashes with studies that say bike lanes actually make the roads safer by forcing drivers (sensible ones, at least) to slow down and avoid potential vehicular manslaughter charges. Rhetorically, the administration’s charge of bike lanes being some form of diversity, equity, and inclusion makes no sense. If riding a bike is so easy, then how can we classify it as unique enough to be diverse? Children ride bikes. It’s far less exotic than, say, operating a motorcycle, which takes a special license in every state. Maybe if we had a dedicated lane for a penny-farthing , I’d buy this explanation. If I were tooling around on one of those, I’d never get where I was going, because scores of beautiful women would be stopping me every few feet. Conservative disapproval for bike lanes stems from a blinkered, irrational view of culture, and more accurately, masculinity. Trumpists have teased Joe Biden and Pete Buttigieg for riding bikes. But I’ve been teased for not being able to ride a bike. Shouldn’t I be lauded for my commitment to machismo? My belief in the petrol-powered conveyance deserves commendation. My parents’ inattention to my development actually made me cooler, right? If anything, I’m the diversity in this scenario. I can’t use a bike lane. I’ve been excluded from significant parts of the road. I can’t even walk in the bike lane. I should be furious, writing pointed, profane letters to my city councilperson, begging them to release me from my shackles. Or better yet, I should demand the city taxpayers pay for me to take bike lessons, so I can be accommodated. I’m the weirdo here. The one who has to explain my predicament, to feel excluded from the general population. Except, I’m not going to complain. I might seethe when I have to swerve to avoid a biker. I might slam on my brakes when I try to turn right and a Schwinn comes screaming through the crosswalk. Maybe I complain for a living on the internet, but I’m also a responsible citizen of the world. I see the obvious benefits of bike access for those that choose to do it, for fitness or for affordability.

events.title: ‘Trump accounts’ promise to mint child millionaires. Experts have their doubts
events.summary: President has hyped growth of federal investment accounts to help US children – for his own political gain Since returning to the White House, Donald Trump has scrapped rules that made childcare more affordable and pushed to cut funding for the nation’s public schools . But with midterm elections fast approaching and his approval ratings very low, the US president has repeatedly trumpeted a two-month-old program designed to help the nation’s children. That program, unhumbly named “ Trump accounts ”, calls for the federal government to give a one-time $1,000 seed deposit to every newborn whose family applies. In campaign speeches this summer , Trump has sought to milk these accounts for maximum political advantage, making big promises about how much these accounts will help the nation’s children. In a speech in Las Vegas last month, Trump hailed the program, saying: “It’s really giving [children] a head start on the American dream… They start off with $1,000 … and they can end up with $100,000, $200,000, $300,000” and if the stock market booms, “you’d end up with $1m”. With these accounts, Trump seems to want to come across as a Santa Claus stuffing $1,000 into every newborn’s stocking (although that money comes from the federal government). He and other Republicans boast that these accounts will significantly lift up all children, including children from low-income families, and also narrow the wealth gap between rich and poor. When Trump kicked off these accounts in early July, the treasury department said : “Trump Accounts level the playing field by allowing every parent to invest in their children’s future, not just wealthy families with trust funds.” A big problem, however, is that many economists say Trump’s claims about these accounts are vastly exaggerated or false. As Trump seeks to excite voters about these accounts, he has hyped how much they will grow, especially with regard to non-affluent families who don’t have the wherewithal to deposit money into these tax-deferred accounts to help their children. In his speeches, Trump sometimes gives the inaccurate impression that a newborn’s account with a $1,000 seed deposit will mushroom to $200,000 or $300,000 by the time the child turns 18, even when that child’s family doesn’t have money to make subsequent deposits. What’s more, “Trump accounts” are likely to increase, not decrease, the wealth gap between rich and poor. These accounts have definite tax advantages for wealthier families, who, unlike most low-income or working-class families, are able to make the maximum $5,000 deposit allowed each year into these tax-deferred accounts. It’s the families rich enough to contribute $5,000 a year who could see their children’s accounts grow to $200,000 or $300,000, far outstripping the accounts of children from poorer families. “This policy is not about giving poor kids a leg up. It’s more likely to widen the gap between rich and poor,” said Justin Wolfers, an economics professor at the University of Michigan, in a video . Kush Desai, a White House spokesperson, said in an email: “Trump Accounts are already shaping up to make a generational difference for working-class children who have not historically benefitted from traditional tax advantaged accounts.” He noted that the billionaires Michael Dell and Ray Dalio, as well as multinational corporations, have “pledged to donate billions of dollars of their wealth to the Trump Accounts of working-class children”. Desai rejected any assertions that the program would increase inequality, saying: “High income parents have always had an array of tools to grow wealth for their kids, but Trump Accounts are giving middle class parents the same opportunity – with billionaires chipping in to help. Only a moron would argue billionaires giving money away to working-class kids will worsen inequality.” The Trump administration has hyped the accounts with extremely optimistic claims. A White House website forecasts that many children with “Trump accounts” will have $271,000 in their account by age 18 and $13m by age 55. That sounds fabulous, but according to Wolfers, those big numbers are based on an impressive 10% annual rate of return for decades – a rate of return that is extraordinarily hard to achieve year after year. Moreover, those higher numbers are for children whose parents put in $5,000 annually until age 18, and then $7,000 a year when their children are in their 20s. Wolfers derided these White House estimates, saying in his video: “They’re ridiculous, they’re dishonest and they’re misleading.” Administration officials defended their estimates of how much the accounts would grow, saying those estimates are “not dissimilar to similar projections issued by retirement account providers”. In his speeches, Trump omits something important: he fails to note that for families unable to contribute beyond the initial $1,000 seed deposit, that amount would, according to White House estimates , grow to $6,000 by age 18.

events.title: Many professionals take continuing education. Let’s add etiquette classes | Gene Marks
events.summary: Many professionals take continuing education. Let’s add etiquette classes This type of training is needed now more than ever, as the American workplace gets more and more diverse A s a certified public accountant, I’m required to earn at least 80 hours every two years of continuing professional education credits. Many other professions and trades, including lawyers, healthcare professionals, engineers, electricians, plumbers and certain contractors, have similar requirements. It’s a good idea. These professional requirements often also include ethics training. That’s a good idea too. But just getting a refresher on ethics isn’t enough. Something else is needed – something that’s even more important: etiquette. One venture capital firm is trying to address that problem. According to a recent story , the firm conducts an “etiquette finishing school” for startup founders and tech entrepreneurs so that they can “learn how to dress and socialize, as well as how to overcome their fear of fish eggs”. Among the topics covered are the importance of wearing a suit and tie to a presentation, understanding how to “approach different rooms”, selecting wines and how to eat caviar. While I’m sure this may be important for some, it’s completely valueless for most. Etiquette goes way beyond fish eggs. It’s becoming a critical management skill. The Encyclopedia Britannica defines etiquette as a system of rules and conventions that regulate social and professional behavior. According to them, “in any social unit there are accepted rules of behavior upheld and enforced by legal codes; there are also norms of behavior mandated by custom and enforced by group pressure.” Etiquette isn’t just about dressing or socializing – or eating caviar. It’s about saying please and thank you. It’s about being on time for meetings. It’s about putting your phone away when having an in-person conversation and letting another driver merge in front of you in traffic. Etiquette means keeping your shoes and socks on your feet during a flight and not bringing a smelly food on the plane. It’s holding the door for the next person. It’s listening to your music in a public place with earbuds. It’s not commenting on a person’s appearance, skin color or sexual orientation. It means understanding and respecting another person’s point of view, regardless of how much you disagree. Etiquette is simply learning how to live and work with people who are different from you. This type of training is needed now more than ever. The American workplace is far more diverse than it was a few generations ago – not just racially, but religiously, culturally, politically and generationally. Women make up roughly half the workforce. Four generations can find themselves working under the same roof. Employees have different religions, sexual orientations, political beliefs and ideas about what constitutes acceptable behavior. Everybody has their thing. How owners, managers and colleagues respond to someone else’s thing is etiquette. For a business to succeed, managers need to not only be versed in their technical requirements, but they have to be skilled at understanding cultures, religious beliefs, political leanings, attitudes, backgrounds and modes of dress. A conservative Christian manager needs to know how to respectfully manage a Muslim employee. A progressive manager needs to know how to respectfully manage a Maga employee. A 25-year-old needs to work with a 65-year-old – and vice versa. This isn’t about making everyone nicer. It’s about making people easier to work with … and therefore more productive. How to help resolve these differences? Lower the temperature? Get along better? One big step would be to expand on that VC firm’s “etiquette finishing school” idea. No, not how to pair wines. But to better know how to behave with others who are different. To show them respect. And why not start with the millions of professionals in this country who are required to take continuing professional education in order to maintain their business licenses? Technical expertise is important. But if we’re already forcing professionals to spend dozens of hours in classrooms, I’d happily trade four of them for something that might actually make us better at dealing with one another. A four-hour class in etiquette isn’t going to solve the world’s problems. But, like any course, something will be remembered. Something will rub off on its participants. And that something may help ease conflict. Sure, it’s easier to succeed in the professional world by choosing the right wine and wearing the right tie. But then again, learning the etiquette so that you can understand, respect and work with your team is even more valuable, not only for business but for the world at large.

In 1858 he imagined the replacement of intellectual property with “socialised knowledge”, which would merge into a “general intellect”, blowing the foundations of capitalism sky high. events.title: Fighting continues between Yemen gov’t forces, Houthis: What is the latest?
events.summary: Yemen’s government forces and Saudi Arabia carry out air attacks to stop Houthis’ advance amid deteriorating humanitarian situation. Fighting has intensified on several fronts in Yemen as the government forces have carried out air attacks on Houthi positions in attempts to retake Mocha, days after the Iran-backed group captured the strategic port city, tightening its grip on the Red Sea – a vital shipping lane. The Houthis, also known as Ansar Allah (supporters of God), have accused Saudi Arabia of launching more than 100 air attacks on Yemen within the past 48 hours. list 1 of 3 Iran-backed Houthis seize strategic Mayun Island: Can they hold it? list 2 of 3 Will the Houthi attacks activate the Mecca Pact? list 3 of 3 Will Houthi advances in Yemen give Iran leverage in its war with the US? Saudi Arabia backs the internationally recognised government, which has described the latest fighting as a “battle for survival”. The fighting has forced tens of thousands of Yemenis from their homes, including more than 2,000 who headed to Djibouti. What is the latest situation on the ground? What is the Saudi role in the conflict, and how has Iran responded? What is the latest situation on the ground? On Saturday, Yemeni government forces said they had launched air attacks on Houthi fighters along the Red Sea coast after the group seized full control of the strategic shoreline. Yemen’s government news agency, Saba, reported that “the armed forces destroyed vehicles and weapons and killed members of the Houthi terrorist militia backed by the Iranian regime” near the port city of Mocha. The spokesperson for the government forces, Majed Abdullah al-Nazili, said they also struck the Houthis’ “vehicles and members” on the Mocha-Dhubab road, 11km (7 miles) from the city, according to Saba. The government’s attacks came after the Houthis captured Mocha on Thursday and the island of Mayyun (also known as Perim) on Friday, completing their hold on the Bab al-Mandeb strait, a narrow waterway vital to global oil shipping. On Sunday, Sultan al-Arada, a member of Yemen’s Presidential Leadership Council (PLC) and governor of Marib, said government forces that withdrew from the west coast are currently regrouping in Marib and will return to the battlefield. In an interview with state-run Saba TV, al-Arada described what happened on the coast as “painful and unfortunate”, but said such setbacks were part of the nature of war. Al-Arada accused the Houthis of bringing the peace process to a dead end and “forcing the option of war” back on Yemen. He said government forces were continuing to fight on several fronts and that the ultimate objective in Marib and elsewhere remained “the restoration of the capital, Sanaa”. “The forces that withdrew are now rearranging themselves, and they will return to the battle again in one form or another,” he said. The Yemeni military’s reserve Nation Shield Force also claimed on Sunday that the reserve’s 6th Brigade had downed five drones during clashes in the al-Aghbara area, according to a report by Turkish state-run Anadolu news agency. Separately, the September Net website, which is affiliated with the army of the internationally recognised Yemeni government, reported that air forces conducted a series of air raids against Houthi targets across the country, saying equipment had been destroyed and Houthi fighters killed, but gave no further details on the number of casualties. Reporting from Sanaa, Yemen, Al Jazeera’s Yousef Mawry said the government forces are trying to recapture territory near the key city of Mocha from the Houthis. The Al Jazeera correspondent said Saudi Arabia is carrying out air attacks, mainly against Houthi military advances. “There have been 129 air strikes on the areas that have recently fallen to the Ansar Allah, including areas in the north where the Houthi group is trying to make advances into the city of Marib, a Yemeni government stronghold.” Mawry said Houthi military buildups in Taiz have also been hit. He added that there are also reports of clashes on the outskirts of Marib, a government-held city considered to be the economic hub of Yemen. “Whoever controls it, controls Yemen’s revenue stream,” he said. Mohammed al-Basha, founder and lead analyst of the Basha Report Risk Advisory, told Al Jazeera that political infighting and division within the government forces are stymying the fight against the fast-moving Houthis. “You’re not going to be able to defeat the Houthis with a split command and control with eight armies sort of competing over influence,” he said. He blamed infighting among government forces as a reason for the Houthis’ military gains. “They’re finger-pointing and blaming each other,” he added. Which are the main front lines in Yemen? The primary active front lines in the latest escalation involve intense fighting between the Iran-backed group and forces aligned with the internationally recognised Yemeni government.

events.title: YouTuber Markiplier's movie made over $50 million. Here's his advice for creators looking to level up.
events.summary: YouTube creator Markiplier, whose real name is Mark Fischbach. Natasha Campos/Getty Images for Mark 'Markiplier' Fischbach YouTuber Markiplier independently released a box-office hit, "Iron Lung," earlier this year. He hopes more content creators will try to take on Hollywood projects without ceding control. He said YouTubers are a "powerful entity that hold sway and a lot of eyeballs." YouTuber Markiplier thinks more creators can break into Hollywood without giving up control. The 37-year-old put it to the test earlier this year, when he wrote, directed, and starred in the film "Iron Lung." He funded the movie's low 7-figure budget himself, and it became a box-office hit that grossed over $50 million worldwide. His takeaway was that more creators should try to enter traditional media on their own, so long as they're ready to learn and wear many hats — and take on their own financial risk. "In Hollywood, it is kind of like a foregone conclusion that you'll have to give up all control to be able to do anything," the YouTuber, whose real name is Mark Fischbach, told Business Insider. "I'm like, 'No, I don't think that should be.'" A decade ago, when social media was still an emergent format, many influencers viewed a TV show deal or a movie role as a sign they'd made it. Content creators like Liza Koshy and Bretman Rock signed on to do TV shows, but YouTube success didn't always translate to TV ratings, and the results were mixed. For every web series that became a TV darling, like Comedy Central's "Broad City," there was a project that stalled out and was canceled, such as NBC's late-night show from YouTuber Lilly Singh. YouTube's gains in recent years have flipped the creator-to-TV pipeline. YouTube has become the top destination on US TV screens, reaching over 14% market share and crushing competitors like Netflix and Disney, according to Nielsen. Former TV stars like Don Lemon, Alton Brown, and Tucker Carlson are building large audiences as independent creators on YouTube and other platforms. The shift in audience to YouTube has given its top creators more power relative to Hollywood, said Fischbach, who has nearly 40 million subscribers. "YouTubers as a conglomerate are this powerful entity that hold sway and a lot of eyeballs are always on them," he said. Creators have power, but distributing a film in theaters or selling a TV show is a different skillset entirely. Fischbach thinks creators, who are used to mastering new formats and come from a DIY culture, can learn what they need to. "Learning things is the most effective way to do more," he said. "I'm playing catch-up all the time, but the more I think about it ahead of time, the more I learn beforehand, the better it'll be." That doesn't mean it's not difficult. Fischbach said even offering a digital version of "Iron Lung" on YouTube — his native platform — has come with its own set of headaches. "Even with my exclusivity deal with YouTube for distribution digitally, there's a lot that I had to learn for even setting up with their system," he said. "It's not like YouTube where you can just upload a video." Successfully pushing through the busy work and other industry red tape was part of what he wanted to prove. "I felt like it was symbolically important to carry it from start to finish" and "show that it could be done," he said. He thinks other creators can pull off the same feat if properly motivated, particularly as industry players like AMC Theaters offer new ways for independent stars like Taylor Swift to release movies in theaters. "There are a lot of creators out there that have the ability to take hold of a project and steer it correctly with their own vision," he said. "They have to expect a lot more out of themselves, and they have to do a lot more work, but at the end of the day, it'll be their vision, and it'll be something unique that only they have created." That said, Hollywood is littered with over a century of would-be movie moguls who thought they had the perfect idea, and there have been plenty of creator projects — even recently — that have failed to translate a massive social audience into another medium. For Markiplier, taking on the challenge, even with real financial risk, is part of what drives him creatively. "I really find purpose in the creative process itself," he said, noting he's not trying to step aside and hand over his business to an outside team. "My objective is not to become an empire," he added. "When I'm done, my YouTube channel will be done. It doesn't go any farther than that, mostly just because I love making things." events.title: A 43-year-old with colon cancer used AI in 3 ways to help make treatment a little easier
events.summary: Russ Read-Barrow was diagnosed with colon cancer. Russ Read-Barrow Russ Read-Barrow was diagnosed with stage 4 colon cancer after seeing blood in his poop. Using Claude, he built a chemotherapy symptom tracker to help him recall what made him feel better. Read-Barrow asks AI to create a summary of his health history for new medical providers. Russ Read-Barrow has been living with incurable stage four colon cancer for five years. The 43-year-old former PR director and father of two from the UK was diagnosed with the disease in 2021. After seeing blood in his poop around six times over the course of a few weeks, he got a colonoscopy. With multiple rounds of chemotherapy and surgeries to remove cancerous cells from his colon, liver, and later his lungs, Read-Barrow's doctors have stopped the cancer from spreading further since 2022. He still needs regular chemotherapy, roughly every three months, to slow cell division and prevent further growth in his lungs and liver. "The chemo I'm having now is doing a good job of keeping it under control, but at some point that'll change and I'll have to have something else," Read-Barrow told Business Insider. Over the years, Read-Barrow has experimented with using AI to help manage the symptoms , medications, and emotional challenges that have become part of his life. In 2025, he launched a side project called FcancerwithAI, a blog where he shares his story and the AI cancer tools he's built. "I'm not saying AI is going to cure cancer. I'm saying it's going to help me remember what my consultant said, spot patterns in my side effects, and maybe give me back some control in a situation where control is basically an illusion," he wrote in a blog post . He hopes that by sharing what has helped him, he can help others, as rates of colon cancer cases in those under 50 have risen since the mid-1990s, making it the deadliest cancer in this age group. However, if spotted early, the survival rate for colon cancer is high, meaning, like Read-Barrow, more and more people are living with cancer as a chronic illness. Here are three ways Read-Barrow has used AI to manage his ongoing cancer treatment . Chemotherapy symptom tracker Russ-Barrow will need chemo for the foreseeable future. Afterwards, he typically experiences side effects like fatigue, nausea, and changes to his mood and sleep habits, which can be hard to cope with. "The hardest part day-to-day is trying to manage the energy windows I do have," he said. He started recording a 30-second voice note chronicling his symptoms each day following chemo, and wearing a WHOOP health tracker . He did this for three cycles of chemo and plugged his information into Claude to spot patterns in how he felt and what exacerbated or eased symptoms. "I found it really useful," he said. The data showed that by around day four after his treatment, he would go from feeling relatively normal to exhausted. "If you see that over time happening again and again, you can sort of deal with it better because you know it's going to come and you don't think, 'Oh God, what's happening?'" he said. Subsequently, he started asking the AI to pick out 10 things he should remember before starting his next round of chemo. One of the things it reminded him was that an anti-nausea medication he tried had helped. "You don't keep a record, you won't remember. You think you will, but give it three months and life will take over and you won't," he said. A medical history research assistant Read-Barrow uploaded all of his medical records to Gemini Notebook (formerly Notebook LM). The AI is designed to answer questions, spot trends, and create content such as presentation decks based only on files the user uploads. He uses it as a "centralized hub" for all of his medical records, which means he can access test results, doctor's notes or any other medical data within seconds. "It saves me from the massive admin headache of digging through folders every time I see a specialist," he said. Getting new people up to speed When signing up for a gym, getting a treatment such as a massage, or seeing any kind of doctor, they typically ask for your medical history. However, when you have a complex chronic illness like cancer, that history can be lengthy and painful to recount. He found a solution by asking Gemini Notebook to summarize his health history in 500 words, which he can pass on. Read-Barrow is aware that not everyone would feel comfortable sharing so much personal information with AI platforms, but for him, the benefits outweigh the risks. "I've got terminal cancer. What's the worst that can bloody happen?" he said. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Abu Dhabi's new off-plan mortgage framework expected to support property market
events.summary: Abu Dhabi 's new off-plan mortgage framework is expected to help buyers and developers by providing clarity on mortgages and boost investor confidence in the emirate's property market, according to analysts. The regulation allows a buyer who has already paid 50 per cent of the home's price to arrange a mortgage against their property during construction, rather than waiting until building is complete. "Adrec's capability to register mortgages against off-plan units has been operational since March 2026, " it said in responses to The National . "Since then, Adrec has engaged relevant developers and financial institutions on the requirements for implementing the service." The first live registration followed once those requirements had been completed, it added. The move is expected to make the property market less exclusive, as well as enhance buyer confidence and reduce transaction friction at handover. "By facilitating mortgages earlier during the construction phase, as opposed to only on handover, investors will be able to purchase off-plan properties with more certainty of the source of funds for future stage payments, making it easier to plan financially," said Matthew Green, head of research at CBRE Middle East and North Africa. "Whilst there are obviously restrictions in place, specifically in terms of the 50 per cent limit for payments and which developers and financial institutions are eligible to participate, we would expect to see this market evolve further over time, becoming more widely available." It will also help increase property transactions and widen the scope of potential source markets, he added. The introduction of the new framework comes as demand for off-plan property remains strong in the emirate, latest data from the Abu Dhabi Real Estate Centre shows. Of the total residential sales of Dh70.4 billion ($19 billion) recorded in Abu Dhabi in the first half of the year, off-plan transactions accounted for 89 per cent. Overall, market activity remains strong despite uncertainty stemming from the Iran war. Abu Dhabi's total real estate transactions in the first six months rose 112 per cent year-on-year to hit Dh117 billion, with transaction volumes rising 61.7 per cent to 16,838, Adrec said. Mortgages climbed by a third to Dh26.7 billion across 8,876 transactions, the data shows. Abu Dhabi's residential pipeline for 2026-2030 stands at about 36,900 homes under construction, with apartments accounting for 66 per cent and villas 33 per cent, while serviced apartments represent 1 per cent, Knight Frank said. Greater flexibility for buyers Both buyers and developers will benefit from the new regulation, said Farooq Syed, chief executive of Springfield Properties. "For buyers ... access to mortgage financing before handover provides greater flexibility in managing the remaining construction instalments and final payment. It also gives buyers more certainty around their financial commitments as they move closer to completion." For developers, the framework could support a broader base of qualified buyers, improve visibility over future payments and reduce the risk of buyers facing liquidity pressure towards the later stages of construction, Mr Syed added. Property developer Aldar has already said it offers mortgage financing on an off-plan property for its customers under Adrec's newly launched framework, with Abu Dhabi Commercial Bank the lender. The framework provides "greater clarity and protection for buyers, lenders and developers", and improves investor confidence in the emirate's property sector, said Andrew Laver, director of Cavendish Maxwell in Abu Dhabi. "It enhances transparency by allowing mortgage interests to be recorded in the Initial Real Estate Register before completion."

The attack on Sunday in the city’s Tal al-Hawa neighbourhood had dismembered the bodies of the deceased, health officials said, appealing to the public for information that could help identify them. list 1 of 2 Trump says a unified Ireland would be ‘fantastic’ during Irish visit list 2 of 2 Gaza genocide documentary ‘NAZA’ wins Special Jury Prize at Venice Footage circulating on social media and verified by Al Jazeera showed the targeted vehicle mangled and gutted, its roof and doors torn away. The strike is the latest in a wave of near-daily Israeli attacks on the war-ravaged, besieged Palestinian territory since a “ceasefire” was agreed by Israel and Hamas last October. More than 1,300 Palestinians have been killed in Israeli attacks across Gaza since the United States-brokered “truce” began, according to health authorities. During a visit to Ireland on Saturday, Trump defended his administration’s record on Gaza. “We put out the fire, and we got all the hostages back. events.title: My listing sat for 4 months. Marketing it as a multigenerational home got 2 offers in a day.
events.summary: Scheryl W. Glanton outside the property she sold as a multi-generational home. Courtesy of Scheryl W. Glanton Real estate agent Scheryl W. Glanton had trouble selling a 5,100-square-foot home with seven bedrooms. She had an "aha moment" and repositioned the property as a multi-generational home . Offers arrived within 24 hours, and Glanton is awaiting closing later this month. This story is based on an interview with Scheryl W. Glanton , 74, a real estate agent from Philadelphia . It has been edited for length and clarity. It was getting frustrating. Despite at least 20 showings of my listing in suburban Philadelphia, no one made an offer. We put the 5,100-square-foot Tudor-style property, built in 1925, on the market in April 2026. I hoped it would sell relatively quickly for the $1m asking price. It was an estate sale, the area had good schools, and the neighborhood was highly sought after. Do you live in a multi-generational household? Please email Jane Ridley at jridley@businessinsider.com to share your story with Business Insider. However, whenever I asked the buyers' agents why their clients weren't interested, they said the same thing: "It's too much house." They said the seven-bedroom, five-and-a-half-bathroom home was too large for one family, regardless of whether they were planning to have more kids. I decided to market it as a multigenerational home Glanton, who has worked in real estate for seven-and-a-half years. Courtesy of Scheryl W. Glanton Everything else — such as its long history, a third-of-an-acre plot, stone walls, and light interior — made it a beautiful option. Four months went by, and there was no movement. Then, in August, I had what can only be described as an "aha moment." The three-story house had two distinct wings and included two sitting rooms on the second floor, two en-suite bedrooms, and a Jack-and-Jill bathroom. It also had two separate entrances, two staircases, and a four-car garage. The place struck me as being perfectly set up for multi-generational living. If I wanted a sale, I needed to lower the price to $875K and pivot. So I repositioned the listing. This time, I marketed it toward young parents and grandparents who wanted to be under the same roof with privacy, too. I got offers immediately Within a day, I got two offers from multigenerational families , with one on hold in case they fell through. The successful buyers, who are paying close to the asking price, were a couple from Los Angeles, their two children, and their aging parents from Indiana. They'd decided to settle in Philadelphia because of a job move, a big relocation for everybody. Glanton has spotted a trend toward multi-generational living. Courtesy of Scheryl W. Glanton After seven-and-a-half years as a real estate agent , I've realized every property is different to me, and every house is personal. It's reinforced my belief that people want to live how they want to live. It has nothing to do with the house, as much as the lifestyle. I always focus on that. There is definitely a trend in the US toward three — or even four — generations living together, whether in a compound, the same house, a duplex, or a triplex. It might be connected to affordability, but I specialize in luxury real estate. Something else is going on. As people get older, what choices do they make about living? One of the most important concerns these days is childcare and eldercare. Multi-generational living can be the sweet spot. There's clearly a market. As the old saying goes, it's the market that speaks. Read the original article on Business Insider
